journeys.lens: End-to-End Lived Experience: The 5 Promised Moments and the Journey's Emotional Arc
journeys.summary: Argus ships a technically sound platform (tests pass, context chains type-safely, outputs are structured) but systematically undersells its core value proposition across the user journey. The philosophy promises five transformational moments: problem reframing, strategy clarity, risk discovery, convergence achievement, and meta-learning. Code implements the data pipelines for these moments but omits the UX choreography that would *signal* them to users. Users experience "analyze → output → download" rather than "aha → clarity → discovery → convergence → wisdom." The product's strength (rigorous thinking structure) becomes invisible, leaving users with a well-made tool that doesn't feel like the "thinking partner" it claims to be. Trust erodes not from bugs but from unfulfilled emotional promises woven through the documentation.

findings.title: The 5 Moments Are Technically Possible but Not Explicitly Signposted—Users Miss the Emotional Arc
findings.evidence: Argus_Product_Philosophy_v2.md:425-439 defines five transformational moments the product should create. Code implements the underlying structure (ProgressiveFlow.tsx ~2670 lines, progressive-engine.ts, context-chain.ts) but never explicitly surfaces when these moments occur. Example: Moment 1 ('aha, I was solving the wrong problem') happens during runInitialAnalysis when real_question diverges from surface_task, but the UI treats it as routine analysis output, not a breakthrough. Moment 5 ('the process itself was the value') should trigger deep reflection at voyage end; no reflection UI exists. Users get the data but not the *recognition* of its significance.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Domain audits validate structure: 'Does reframe produce hidden_questions?' (yes). They don't validate emotional impact: 'Do users *feel* the reframe?' (probably not without explicit framing). The philosophy is aspirational UX; domain audits measure functional UX. A system can have correct outputs and missed moments simultaneously.
findings.impact: Users complete voyages feeling mildly satisfied rather than transformed. Internally they may have discovered something profound, but externally they see 'analysis done, here's your document.' The product fails to build the trust that comes from *recognizing* thinking has shifted. Churn risk: users don't return because they don't feel like the tool changed them; they just made a decision.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit 'moment markers' in the UI: (1) When real_question diverges from surface_task by >30%, show a brief 'Wait, that's different from what you asked' celebration. (2) When governing_idea solidifies, render it with animation/ceremony as 'Here's the thread holding this together.' (3) Highlight unexpected risks with 'Nobody usually sees this coming, but...' (4) On convergence_score jumps, show 'Team just aligned another 15%.' (5) At voyage end, mandatory (not optional) reflection: 'What surprised you most about your thinking?' Store and surface on revisits. These are seconds of UX, not hours of engineering, but they close the gap between what the system does and what the user *knows* it did.

findings.title: Context Chain Is Typed But Not Visually Traced—Users Can't See How Input Became Output
findings.evidence: context-chain.ts (buildReframeContext, injectReframeContext) and context-builder.ts establish technical wiring: original problem → reframed question → governing idea → execution steps. All type-safe, all structured. But ProgressiveFlow has no UI that shows users this causal path. When the final document arrives, it includes no breadcrumb like 'Your initial assumption was [X], which led us to question [Y], which reframed the core challenge to [Z], which drove this execution structure.' The philosophy (Product_Philosophy_v2.md:2.2, '맥락 누적 체인') promises users will 'see the context chain with their eyes.' Code hides it.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Correctness audit: 'Does reframe output feed recast input?' (yes, via type-safe handoff). Traceability audit: 'Can a user verify the causal chain?' (no, it's opaque data inside the system). Provenance is invisible.
findings.impact: Users over-trust or under-trust without basis. When the final governing_idea emerges, they can't verify it's actually addressing their real problem because they can't trace the reasoning backward. This breaks the 'Argus makes my thinking transparent' promise. Worse, if the output misses the mark, users blame themselves ('I must have communicated poorly') rather than the system ('the reasoning chain went off track'). Lost opportunities for course correction.
findings.recommendation: Implement an 'Origin Trace' feature toggled on in the final outputs (Project Brief, Agent Spec). Each major decision (governing_idea, key_assumptions, critical_path) includes a collapsed 'Why?' accordion showing: source phase → contributing evidence → user input that led to it. Optional, but visible by default on first view. This lets power users audit the logic without cluttering the main document. Example: 'Governing Idea: Focus on customer retention rather than acquisition. Why? Because reframe identified that your hidden assumption was growth = new customers, but user feedback (#5 from Q&A) suggested churn is the real issue.'

findings.title: Ship's Log (Logbook) Is Positioned as Footnote, Not Protagonist—Process Value Is Opt-In
findings.evidence: FinalCard.tsx:76-83 shows the voyage log behind a checkbox: 'Also include the decision log when copying/sharing.' Logbook.tsx exists but is a hidden drawer on mobile, lower priority than the clean document. The philosophy (Product_Philosophy_v2.md:3.4, '항해일지와 메타 보정') positions the log as the *primary* artifact where 'this is the asset that lasts'—but code treats it as optional supplementary data. Users see 'Copy Document' as the obvious action; the Log is a power-user discovery.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Completeness audit: 'Can users export the log?' (yes, code exists). Priority audit: 'Is the log positioned as the hero or the sidekick?' (sidekick). The feature exists but is architecturally de-emphasized. This is intentional product design that contradicts the stated philosophy.
findings.impact: Users walk away with a 30-page decision document but never internalize the 3-page journey that got there. They don't accumulate 'thinking patterns.' They don't re-read to notice 'oh, this is the third time I've worried about stakeholder misalignment'—because the log is hidden. The core thesis ('the process is the deliverable') goes unrealized. Next voyage, they restart from zero instead of learning.
findings.recommendation: Invert the final-output experience: Make 'Your Decision Record' (the log) the primary display at voyage completion. Show it as 'Here's what you learned.' Then offer 'For Sharing: Clean Document' as a secondary download. Psychologically, this tells users 'your insight matters more than the artifact.' On revisits, surface 'Patterns from your last 3 voyages: You often worry about [X], rarely about [Y].' This compounds the value and builds meta-strategic learning.

findings.title: Backtracking Costs Are Hidden—Users Don't Know Navigation Will Trigger Full Re-Analysis
findings.evidence: ProgressiveFlow supports backward navigation (edit reframe, re-answer Q&A, rerun analysis) via 'onMore' and 'onRevisit' buttons in VoyagePrepSummary. But there's no UX signpost of 'if you edit the real question, we'll re-analyze everything (est. 30-40 seconds) and may update your execution plan.' Users who hit 'Back' expecting a 10-second tweak face a spinner and may abandon thinking the system is broken. No confirmation modal, no impact preview, no cost estimate.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Functionality audit: 'Can users navigate backward?' (yes). Friction audit: 'Do users understand the cost of navigation?' (no). This is a hidden-assumptions problem, not a missing feature.
findings.impact: Abandonment: users fear backtracking and stick with sub-optimal directions. Confusion: users re-navigate thinking it's 'free' and get annoyed at latency. The philosophy ('repeat until convergent') assumes users will iterate; hidden costs prevent that.
findings.recommendation: Before executing backward navigation, show a modal: 'Edit Real Question? This will re-analyze the team (est. 30s) and may update your execution plan. Your Q&A answers stay, but analysis refreshes.' Include a 'Preview Changes' toggle (cheap API call showing what would shift). This educates users about the topology and makes iteration feel intentional, not accidental.

findings.title: Persona Feedback Loop Never Closes—Users Don't See If Their Edits Actually Satisfied Decision-Makers
findings.evidence: PersonaFeedbackStep (components/workspace/progressive/) generates DM feedback with accuracy_ratings stored in usePersonaStore. But no UI offers 'You responded to the CFO's cost concern—let's check: would she approve now?' There's no re-test flow. Users see feedback, edit their plan, and move on without confirmation that feedback-driven edits landed. The philosophy (Product_Philosophy_v2.md:2.3, 'Rehearsal Intelligence') promises a tight feedback loop; the code doesn't wire it closed.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Output audit: 'Does rehearse generate feedback?' (yes). Closure audit: 'Does the user verify edits landed?' (no). The loop is architecturally open.
findings.impact: Feedback becomes noise, not signal. Users either over-correct (defensive bloat) or ignore it (false confidence). The most powerful feature—simulated stakeholder validation—goes underutilized because users don't see its effect.
findings.recommendation: Add a post-refinement 'Verification Gate': After edits, offer 'Check: Will [Persona] approve now?' (30s re-run of persona-feedback on updated plan). Display side-by-side 'Before/After Reaction' so users see impact. Make this default-on for at least the first 2-3 iterations. This closes the feedback loop and trains users that Argus is a *collaborative* tool, not a 'analyze once and ship' tool.

findings.title: Landing Page + Hero Flow Choreography Creates False Intimacy—Team Avatars Suggest Orchestrated Collaboration; Reality Is a Single LLM Call
findings.evidence: app/workspace/page.tsx:468-499 (HeroFlow 'assembling' phase) shows team member avatars staggered-animating as if being 'assembled.' The copy says 'Team assembled. Analyzing the situation.' But runInitialAnalysis is a single LLM call generating a snapshot; no orchestrated agent work happens. Users see animated team members but then a monolithic 'analyzing...' spinner with no per-agent task visibility. The 'team' vanishes after the animation; it was theatrical, not real.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Correctness audit: 'Does initial analysis produce good snapshots?' (yes). Authenticity audit: 'Do the visuals reflect the actual execution model?' (no). This is a false-promise problem, not a feature problem.
findings.impact: Trust erosion at onboarding. Users expect collaborative intelligence, see team choreography, then get a standard LLM spinner. The positioning ('an AI team watches with you') collides with the reality (a single fast model). Power users shrug; newcomers feel oversold. This hampers the core positioning that Argus is different from 'just asking Claude.'
findings.recommendation: Choose: (a) Make it real: implement actual multi-agent analysis in initial snapshot (each persona submits observations). (b) Be honest: replace team animation with 'Analyzing from multiple perspectives' and drop individual avatars. Better to underpromise and over-deliver. Current hybrid is the worst option.

findings.title: The 4 Output Types (Brief/Chain/Spec/Checklist) Are Static, Not Living—No Accumulation Across Voyages
findings.evidence: FinalCard, progressive-handoff, and export functions generate Project Brief, Prompt Chain, Agent Spec, and Execution Checklist as one-time markdown strings. ROADMAP.md promises these become 'living documents' and 'execution artifacts' (Spec feeds LangGraph, Checklist tracks progress). Current code makes all four read-only downloads. Checklist can't persist checkbox state. Agent Spec is not linted/validated for LangGraph compatibility. No 'next time you run this analysis, it should learn from last time.'
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Artifact completeness: 'Are the 4 outputs structurally correct?' (yes). Lifecycle audit: 'Do these improve over time or on re-entry?' (no). Single-use artifacts don't compound value.
findings.impact: One-off decision tool, not a compounding strategic asset. Users run Argus, ship a plan, never interact with it again. No feedback loop, no multi-run intelligence. The philosophy (ROADMAP.md:569-571) promises 'judgment accumulation from 1000 users' and 'the thinking itself becomes the asset'—but there's no mechanism to surface 'this is your 4th market analysis; last time the CEO doubted ROI, so this time let's preemptively address it.' Each voyage is isolated.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade outputs: (1) Checklist backed by Supabase so completion state persists across sessions. (2) Next-run contextualization: on project re-entry, surface 'Last voyage: CEO was skeptical of timeline. This time?' (3) Multi-voyage patterns: 'You've shipped 5 plans; 3 had stakeholder alignment issues. Pattern?' This converts single outputs into cumulative decision scaffolding and builds network effects.

findings.title: Convergence Score (항로 지수) Is Computed but Hidden—Users Don't Know When to Stop Iterating
findings.evidence: progressive-convergence.ts computes convergence_score and per-stakeholder metrics. RefinementLoopStep UI shows 'unresolved_issues' count but not the trending convergence metric. The philosophy (Product_Philosophy_v2.md:3.4, '항로 지수') promises 'SVG chart showing convergence%; when it hits 80%+, ship.' Code has the calculation; UI barely exposes it.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Data audit: 'Is convergence computed?' (yes). Progress visibility: 'Can users see it trending upward?' (no, it's hidden). This is a presentation gap, not a calculation gap.
findings.impact: Users have no principled stopping point. They iterate either forever or arbitrarily. The voyage metaphor ('tighten until it holds') fails without visible traction. Users over-iterate (wasted time, decision paralysis) or under-iterate (ship with unresolved concerns).
findings.recommendation: Prominent Convergence Gauge in RefinementLoopStep: large display showing 'Convergence: 67%' with statement 'Ready to ship at 80%+.' Show what improved since last iteration. Per-persona breakdown: 'CEO: 45%, CTO: 92%, Design: 88%—focus on finance.' Make the metric the hero, not the fine print.

findings.title: Dual-Mode Architecture (Progressive vs. Legacy 4-Step) Fragments the User Model and Creates No Bridge
findings.evidence: workspace/page.tsx:703-835 maintains two parallel entry points: new sessions → ProgressiveFlow (conversational Q&A + phased analysis); legacy or ?step=reframe param → separate 4-step components (ReframeStep, RecastStep, etc.). Both work, but they're not integrated. No 'import legacy analysis into progressive' flow. No unified mode selection in the UI. Power users encounter friction ('which should I use?'); old users hit a wall ('my old reframe doesn't sync with the new flow').
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Compatibility audit: 'Do both flows work?' (yes). Coherence audit: 'Do they feel like the same product?' (no). This is design-debt that doesn't break anything but creates confusion.
findings.impact: Cognitive load for onboarding. No upgrade path for power users. Lost data reuse across modes. If Progressive is the vision, the old 4-step is a distraction; if 4-step is still valid, there should be a 'choose your voyage style' menu with clear tradeoffs.
findings.recommendation: Commit to one direction: If Progressive is the future, add a 'Bridge' feature to import 4-step outputs into Progressive (ReframeItem → ProgressiveSession conversion). If both coexist, add a unified mode selector: 'Choose Your Voyage: Conversational (Progressive Q&A) or Structured (4-Step Upload)' with tooltips explaining tradeoffs. Don't hide it in undocumented query params.

journeys.the_one_thing: **The product's greatest blind spot is this: it has built a technically sophisticated machine for structured thinking but forgot to *celebrate* when thinking actually happens.** Users complete voyages with richer strategic clarity than they brought, but the UX never says "you see this differently now." The five moments the philosophy promises (reframing, clarity, discovery, convergence, meta-learning) occur in the data, not in the user's conscious experience. Without explicit framing of these moments—a 30-second celebration when the real question diverges from the surface task, a prominent convergence gauge, a post-voyage reflection prompt, a visible causal chain from problem to solution—the product feels like an efficient tool rather than a thinking partner. The lived experience is "I got a better document," not "I understand my problem differently." This gap between architectural sophistication (which domain audits see) and emotional payoff (which users feel) is where Argus leaks trust. Fixing it doesn't require rebuilding; it requires showing users what they've already accomplished.

journeys.lens: Skeptical First-Timer (90-Second Funnel): Do I Get It? Do I Care? Why Not ChatGPT?
journeys.summary: ARGUS lands with a compelling voyage metaphor—'you hold the helm while the team thinks'—and a beautiful landing page. The skeptical first-timer sees this, clicks 'Start' with one sentence, and waits 30 seconds for the AI to 'analyze.' When the results appear, they're well-structured markdown: a 'real question,' hidden assumptions, skeleton steps. But then... what? No dialogue, no branching point, no moment where control feels handed back to the user. Just static text to read. The core issue: the product's narrative promises active partnership ('you steer, we advise') but delivers passive consumption ('here's a structured answer'). By the time the user realizes they need to scroll to see what branching or refinement options exist, they've already experienced 4-5 minutes of interaction with zero moments of agency. The demo scenarios exist but are hidden below the input. The 'real' value (iterative refinement, persona feedback, comparison) comes later. The immediate experience feels like ChatGPT-with-extra-words, not ChatGPT's opposite.
journeys.the_one_thing: The landing narrative and the product experience are fundamentally misaligned. The landing promises 'you captain the ship; we're the harness.' The product delivers 'here's structured thinking; judge it or iterate.' A skeptical first-timer with 2 minutes of patience lands on the voyage metaphor, clicks Start to prove the metaphor works, waits 30 seconds, gets an answer, and sees no clear reason why they didn't just ask ChatGPT. The metaphor is the product's core positioning, but it's not delivered in the first-run experience—it only becomes relevant on the 3rd or 4th refinement loop. This is a churn cliff that's hard to measure because it's not a technical bug; it's a coherence failure between promise and delivery.

findings.title: CRITICAL: The 'Convincing Journey' Metaphor Obscures Rather Than Clarifies The Actual Experience
findings.evidence: README.md (§1-4, voyage structure), Argus_Product_Philosophy_v2.md (§1.1-1.2, Argus/Siren framing), src/app/page.tsx (Act1Voyage: '항해는 왜 종착지에 닿지 못했는가' + 'AI라는 감미로운 목소리에 홀려'), src/app/workspace/page.tsx (HeroFlow component)
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A domain-by-domain audit (landing UX, conversion funnel, UI polish, architecture) stays at the surface level of WHAT the product does. It won't catch the fundamental mismatch between the narrative promise (voyage, decision harness, seizing control back from AI) and the actual lived experience (you type 1 sentence → watch a 20-40 second spinner → get handed 3 static markdown pages). The metaphor creates a false sense of control and partnership when the reality is: your input is inert, the LLM decides everything.
findings.impact: First-timers arrive hyped by the voyage narrative, click 'Start,' watch a loading screen for 30+ seconds, and see a beautifully formatted but fundamentally non-interactive response. The metaphor promised a helm to hold, a team to consult, active dialogue. What they got: a prettier version of ChatGPT with more words. The dissonance between narrative and reality is the churn vector.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) redesign the experience to actually deliver the voyage promise—make the 4 steps interactive, let users steer between them, add decision-maker simulation before final outputs, not after—OR (2) reframe the landing narrative to match reality: position as 'structured thinking companion' not 'you captain the ship.' Currently attempting both and succeeding at neither. The metaphor should serve the experience, not the reverse.

findings.title: The 'First-Run' Experience Has 3+ Separate Unresolved Pathways, None Clearly Winning
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (HeroFlow 145-622): useLegacyMode (lines 644-646), progressiveSession check (line 703), legacy Step-based flow (line 718ff) vs new Progressive flow (line 709ff), demo mode (line 263), plus InitialAnalysis which can fail if parsing breaks
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A UX audit looks at 'does the current happy path work?' It won't ask the harder question: 'which path is supposed to be primary?' The code reveals four overlapping experiences: new users via HeroFlow→ProgressiveFlow, legacy users via ?step= params, returning users (either path), demo users (separate flow). This isn't graceful phasing-out; it's four competing implementations with no clear hierarchy or deprecation story.
findings.impact: Maintenance debt accrues as bugs fix one path then break another. Onboarding becomes ambiguous: do we guide new users to progressive or legacy? Analytics split across funnels. A first-timer hitting a bug in one path doesn't know if it's actually broken or just the old path.
findings.recommendation: Pick ONE primary first-run flow. If progressive is the future (it appears to be, based on recent commits), fully deprecate legacy mode: remove ?step= param handling, remove 4-step tab UI from new sessions. If legacy must co-exist, add explicit branching logic that surfaces the choice to users upfront rather than hiding it in query params.

findings.title: The Landing Page Fails to Set Expectations About the 20-40 Second Synchronous Wait
findings.evidence: src/components/landing/voyage/Act1Voyage.tsx (lines 67-114): epic tone about control vs. src/app/workspace/page.tsx (line 531): '보통 20~40초' appears ONLY after user clicks Start and spinner begins, not before
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The landing copy sets an epic tone—'you hold the helm,' 'the team watches with you.' But the actual product requires a 30-second synchronous wait. This isn't mentioned upfront. A UX audit will check 'is the loading state well-designed?' and miss that the loading state shouldn't exist—or if it does, should be called out on the landing page itself.
findings.impact: Impatient first-timers hit Start, see a team assembling animation, watch blank field spinners, and at 15 seconds think 'is this frozen?' At 25 seconds, they leave. They never get to see outputs or understand what value they might receive.
findings.recommendation: On the landing page, below the 'Start' button, add one sentence: '30-second AI analysis—watch the team assemble and think through your situation.' Alternatively, reduce wait by: (1) streaming partial results to UI faster, (2) pre-computing suggestions, (3) showing clearer progress.

findings.title: The Demo/Interactive Discovery Path Is Shadowboxed—Users Don't Know It Exists Without Scrolling
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 436-454): demo scenarios shown below main input, labeled '처음이라면 — 시나리오로 둘러보기' (New here? Try a sample), only visible after scrolling on mobile
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A UX audit checks 'is the demo easy to find?' and might say yes. But this misses the discovery funnel for skeptical users: they land, see epic copy, try the input, and if that fails, they should have a safe escape hatch. The demo exists but is positioned as secondary, not as the path of least risk.
findings.impact: First-timer: lands → sees promise → finds input → thinks 'risky, I don't know what this does' → clicks Start → waits 30s → gets markdown → unsure if it worked. If they'd clicked demo first, they'd understand the product. But the demo is buried.
findings.recommendation: Redesign idle phase to surface 3 options upfront: (1) Start with real problem, (2) Try sample scenario, (3) Continue past project. Make 'Try a sample' equal visual weight to 'Start.' Or make it the DEFAULT: demo auto-loads → user sees value → clicks 'Try your own.'

findings.title: The Progressive Flow's Invisible Waypoint State Breaks First-Run Expectations
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (ProgressiveLayout, lines 64-77): hasWaypoints checks sess?.waypoints?.length, showRail depends on hasWaypoints OR hasWorkers; waypoints only populated after initial analysis completes (line 235)
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The progressive architecture is sophisticated. But from the user's perspective, once they submit a problem, they're suddenly in an empty 'workspace' with no visible content until AI generates the first waypoint. There's a hidden state transition: HeroFlow → ProgressiveLayout (empty) → first waypoint appears. A UX audit won't catch this confusing middle moment.
findings.impact: First-timers reach the workspace (after 30-second wait) and see: empty left side, empty right sidebar (logbook hasn't populated), no clear next step. They think it crashed or they're in the wrong place. The actual next step (AI will generate a question) isn't communicated.
findings.recommendation: After initial analysis completes, add a transient message: 'Analysis complete. First question loading…' with a spinner. Make the transition from 'empty workspace' to 'first interaction' explicit and expected.

findings.title: The Product Has No Coherent Answer to 'Why Not Just ChatGPT?' at the Moment of First Use
findings.evidence: README.md (§7 'Real Competitor'): explicitly states 'real competitor is just asking ChatGPT directly'; Argus_Product_Philosophy_v2.md (§1.2) promises 'hear without jumping,' but actual experience is: you get output, see static markdown, no intermediate judgment moment
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: An audit focused on features won't ask: 'what does this product prevent me from doing that ChatGPT allows?' The answer is supposed to be: 'prevent jumping at AI answers without judgment.' But the product doesn't prevent jumping—it just formats it nicely. First-timers won't feel the value until their 3rd or 4th refinement loop.
findings.impact: First-timers type a problem, get an answer, don't feel a strong reason to have come here instead of ChatGPT. They'll need repeated use to feel the harness. By then, churn has happened.
findings.recommendation: Add an active judgment moment in first-run. After initial analysis, ask: 'Does this reframing feel right? Would ChatGPT have suggested something different?' This reframes the output from abstract ('structured thinking') to concrete ('I'm making a decision').

findings.title: Error Handling in Hero Flow Silently Breaks If Streaming JSON Parse Fails
findings.evidence: src/lib/partial-analysis.ts (lines 102-117): parsePartialAnalysis() returns potentially empty fields if JSON is malformed; src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 221-228): streaming callback doesn't validate parse success
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Happy-path tests pass. But if LLM returns slightly malformed JSON (extra comma, truncated array), the UI renders blank fields ('Searching...' forever) with no error, no fallback, no retry option.
findings.impact: If an LLM call returns 98% valid JSON, UI hangs with blank fields. User sees 'Searching...' for 5+ minutes, then times out. No clear message, no next action.
findings.recommendation: In streaming callback, after parsing, check if critical fields have content. If stage is 'skeleton' but real_question is empty after 30s, either: show what you have as 'preliminary thinking,' re-prompt with simpler instructions, or show 'results coming slowly—use what we have?'

findings.title: The Quota System Conflates 'Free Trial' with 'Free Tier'—Misaligned Messaging
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 335-342): banner says '로그인 없이 하루 {ANON_LIMIT}회 무료 · 로그인하면 하루 {DAILY_LIMIT}회' (free per day without login); underlying logic is hard tier limit, not countdown
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Copy suggests 'try for free, then upgrade' (trial messaging). Implementation is 'you get X free per day forever' (tier messaging). These signal different value props. Trials convert via urgency; tiers convert via value. This does neither clearly.
findings.impact: Users hit limit and see login CTA. But they don't know: is this artificial (urgent, sign up now) or genuine (I can come back tomorrow). Confusion reduces login intent.
findings.recommendation: If limit is artificial (conversion funnel), say '5 free analyses while you decide' (adds urgency). If genuine, say 'Free plan: 5/day. Login for 20/day.' Currently it's ambiguous.

findings.title: The Product Vision Has Split Into Two Versions (Progressive vs. Legacy) with No Migration Story
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (both ProgressiveFlow and legacy Step components coexist); git history (commit 40da532 refactors toward progressive); ROADMAP.md describes legacy 4-step as primary; philosophy doc describes voyage as core
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: An audit focused on current code won't notice the product is being rewritten mid-flight. The planned product (4 phases, iterative loop) differs from actual product (progressive streaming, branching, logbook). These are two different products sharing one name.
findings.impact: Product feels like a beta being rebuilt. New users see progressive. Returners might see legacy (via bookmarked ?step=). Docs don't match code. Coherence is broken.
findings.recommendation: Commit to one vision. If progressive is future, update docs. If legacy is vision, remove progressive code. Decide and align.

findings.title: The Right Sidebar (Logbook) Represents Real Competitive Advantage but Is Invisible on First Run
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 119-126): Logbook rendered in sticky right rail; showRail depends on hasWaypoints, which only populates after first interaction completes; first-timers see empty right rail
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The logbook (full chart/voyage branches/narrative) is one of Argus's real differentiators vs. ChatGPT—it shows the *thinking path*, not just the output. But first-timers don't see it until they've already interacted once. The value isn't visible in the initial moment of risk/doubt.
findings.impact: First-timer can't see 'oh, I'll have a full audit trail and branching capability' until after they've committed to first step. This should be a selling point in the demo.
findings.recommendation: In demo mode, show a pre-built logbook/branch chart alongside the narrative flow. Let first-timers see: 'this is the audit trail you'll get, with branches you can explore.' Show the competitive difference before asking them to invest 30 seconds.

findings.title: The 'Team Assembly' Animation Doesn't Match What the 'Team' Actually Does
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 468-497): 'Team assembled' animation shows 4 personas with names and roles; src/lib/worker-personas.ts would show these are pre-set templates; but the initial analysis has no actual 'workers'—only the base LLM
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The 'team' concept is core to the voyage metaphor. The animation sells it visually. But on first-run, there's no actual team—no workers deployed, no parallel tasks, no human input solicited. The workers only appear later (in progressive questions, in rehearsal, etc.). The animation is selling a promise that doesn't apply to the immediate experience.
findings.impact: First-timers see '팀이 구성되었습니다. 상황을 분석합니다' (Team assembled. Analyzing situation.) but the team isn't doing anything yet—it's just the base LLM streaming. The metaphor oversells the reality.
findings.recommendation: Either (1) remove the team animation on first run—just show 'Analyzing...' and introduce workers/team when they actually appear, or (2) make the team real: show parallel tasks (one LLM reading situation, another drafting assumptions, etc.) in the spinner UI. Right now it's metaphor without substance.

findings.title: The Marketing Copy Below the Input ('배가 아무리 빨라도, 해도 없이는 표류일 뿐입니다') Only Appears for First-Timers, Not for People Who Need Convincing
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 456-464): bottom marketing text only renders if projects.length === 0 (first-timers); but first-timers are also most impatient—they're the ones least likely to scroll down
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The most persuasive copy in the entire product ('배 없이는...' / 'no map, only drift') is positioned lowest and hidden until projects load. But the users who need to read it (skeptics, first-timers) see it last, if at all. The sales funnel is backwards.
findings.impact: First-timers land → see hero input → might not see the compelling positioning until they've already scrolled past it or given up. Returners, who've already bought in, see it on every session (waste of real estate).
findings.recommendation: Move the positioning copy above the input, not below. Or, show it as a transient tooltip when users hover over the input, or in the error state if they try to submit with empty input.

findings.title: The Workspace Lacks a Clear 'Next Step' Signal After Initial Output
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (lines 115-117): ProgressiveFlow renders without explicit UI prompting what to do next; the 'next question' comes from progressive store, which may be empty on first load
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: After the initial 30-second wait and markdown output, what does the user do? Click a button? Scroll? Wait for more? The product doesn't say. A UX audit focused on the *current* screen will call it 'clean and minimal.' But from the user's perspective, it's unclear.
findings.impact: First-timers complete the initial analysis and sit in silence. They see static text. There's no 'What do you think?' or 'Next question ready' or 'Edit your answer' button visible until they scroll or wait for async load. The momentum is lost.
findings.recommendation: After initial analysis renders, show a prominent footer bar or floating action button: 'Ready for next question' or 'Review & refine' or 'Compare approaches.' Make the next interaction obvious.

findings.title: The Glossary of Nautical Metaphor Is Never Taught to Users—Only in Docs
findings.evidence: README.md (§2-4): explains 항로 재설정 (reframe), 선원 배치 (recast), 리허설 (rehearse), 항로 수정 (refine) as if metaphor is common knowledge; Argus_Product_Philosophy_v2.md (§4.1): 'When a user first encounters the word "항로 재설정," they should understand it means "problem redefinition" without having read the philosophy doc'
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The product names its steps using nautical metaphor (항로, 선원, 항해, 이타카). These are meant to be intuitive, not need learning. But a first-timer reading '항로 재설정' without context might not connect it to 'problem redefinition.' The metaphor is self-referential—it assumes you've already bought into the voyage framing.
findings.impact: Users land on a brand-new product with unfamiliar terminology. The steps should be self-explanatory; instead they require prior knowledge of the metaphor.
findings.recommendation: On first exposure to each step name, show the English translation and a 1-sentence explanation in a tooltip: '항로 재설정 (Reframe) — Uncover the hidden question your situation is really asking.' Make terminology transparent, not mystique.

findings.title: Analytics Tracking Exists but Isn't Wired to Surface Churn Moments
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx (track calls on lines 210, 226, 255, 257, 660); src/lib/analytics.ts would show events like 'workspace_problem_submit', 'first_analysis_start', 'workspace_start_error'; but no events for 'user_saw_output_then_closed,' 'user_waited_30s_then_left,' 'user_didnt_see_logbook'
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Tracking is in place for entry and error, but not for the silent churn moment: when a user completes the initial flow, looks at the output, and closes the tab. There's no event for 'first output viewed' or 'first output engaged' vs. 'abandoned'—so you can't measure where exactly the 90-second funnel breaks.
findings.impact: Leadership sees 'X users started Y analyses' but not 'X users started, Y completed initial view, Z took an action after.' The churn cliff is invisible.
findings.recommendation: Add tracking: (1) 'first_output_rendered' (initial markdown loaded), (2) 'first_output_scrolled' (user scrolled to see full output), (3) 'first_next_step_clicked' (user chose an action: refine, branch, etc.). This surfaces where the funnel breaks.

findings.title: Progressive Questions Are the Real UX, But They're Hidden Behind an Initial 30s Wait and Unlabeled
findings.evidence: src/lib/progressive-engine.ts (buildFlowQuestion, pickNextQuestionType): the progressive question loop is sophisticated—multi-branch, adaptive, worker-inclusive; but the first-timer sees it only after waiting for initial analysis and completing one round trip
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: The actual breakthrough UX (interactive Q&A loop, branching, refinement) is buried 2-3 interactions deep. The first-run experience is: input → wait 30s → see markdown. The second interaction is when the real product starts. A UX audit focused on 'is the flow good?' won't catch that the flow doesn't start until interaction 2.
findings.impact: First-timers judge the product on the *first* interaction (markdown output), not the *real* product (progressive Q&A). They decide in those first 30 seconds + markdown view, before the good UX even starts.
findings.recommendation: Demo the progressive Q&A loop on the landing page or in the sample scenarios. Let first-timers see: 'After this first analysis, you'll get a question to answer, then another—think of it as a dialogue.' This sets expectations for the *real* experience they'll have if they stay past interaction 1.

journeys.lens: Returning Power User — Do accumulated patterns actually respect your time and show value?
journeys.summary: ARGUS collects judgment patterns (override rates, actor preferences, decision trends) and displays them in a "Your Judgment Patterns" card on the Project page. However, these patterns are NOT fed back into subsequent session AI prompts. The promise "사용할수록 똑똑해집니다" (the smarter you get, the more you use it) is partially delivered: past decisions are VISIBLE to the user but not CONSEQUENTIAL to the AI. A returning power user on their 5th project sees their override rate ("수정 44%") but gets the same generic opening questions as a first-timer. The learned moat exists in memory but not in behavior.

findings.title: Judgment patterns collected but not injected into AI prompts
findings.evidence: src/lib/user-context.ts:57-58 (getUserObservations: 'UI 전용 — 설정 페이지에서만... 프롬프트에는 사용하지 않음'); src/lib/progressive-prompts.ts:23 (buildInitialAnalysisPrompt takes only problemText+locale, no userContext); src/lib/agent-tools.ts:151-162 (gatherToolContext only recalls past AGENT work, not user judgment patterns)
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A typical audit focuses on individual domain features (whether sessions work, whether patterns are stored, whether UI shows them). It doesn't check the CROSS-DOMAIN FLOW: whether user-level learned behavior actually PROPAGATES to the AI's next decision point. The stored judgment data and the prompt-building code live in different layers; both can be 'correct' while the integration is missing.
findings.impact: Returning users invest time recording override decisions (AI→Human, Human→AI shifts), and the app celebrates this via 'Your patterns' dashboard cards. But this investment doesn't accelerate or personalize their NEXT session. They re-answer the same opening questions, see the same generic framings, and re-teach the AI their preferences. The moat promise—that the product learns and gets better for you—is broken at the returning-user barrier.
findings.recommendation: Inject userContext (override rate, dominant actor assignment, decision trends) into buildInitialAnalysisPrompt and buildDeepeningPrompt. E.g., if a user has shifted 60% of AI-suggested steps to 'self' (human judgment), the initial skeleton should front-load the self-decision points. If their override rate is <10%, prompt should be more aggressive in providing ready-to-use recommendations rather than open questions.

findings.title: Empty states and onboarding treat returning users the same as first-timers
findings.evidence: src/app/workspace/page.tsx:200-250 (HeroFlow assembles/analyzing/ready phases with no returning-user shortcuts); no 'resume your last pattern' or 'this is similar to Project X' suggestions when creating new session; src/app/project/page.tsx:656-672 (similar-project hint exists but appears AFTER project is selected, not as a discovery aid)
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Onboarding flows are tested as isolated features. A domain audit of 'onboarding' will check: does the text explain the 4 stages? Does the demo play? Does the button link work? It won't test: 'for a user who has 4 completed projects, does the onboarding change to respect their time?' That cross-user, time-aware lens is outside typical domain scope.
findings.impact: Returning users see the same hero flow (HeroFlow idle→assembling→analyzing→ready) every time. No 'Pick a past project to branch from' option, no 'Your last 3 projects were about [market entry / cost reduction / team scaling] — what's this one about?' No resume-session shortcuts. Each session starts from zero, burning user time on re-orientation.
findings.recommendation: In HeroFlow, detect if user.judgments.length > 5 or projects.completed > 2. If true, show: (1) Quick-start card 'Branch from [Last Project]' with single-click resume, (2) 'Similar situations' hint with projects tagged by decision-maker or ai/human ratio, (3) Collapsible 'Your patterns' summary (override rate, dominant actor, decision speed trend). Make it optional (users can still start fresh) but discoverable.

findings.title: recallPastWork function exists but is not surfaced to users
findings.evidence: src/lib/agent-tools.ts:46-90 (recallPastWork finds prior approved agent work by keyword overlap, returns ToolResult); called in gatherToolContext at line 153-154 (only for Lv.2+ agents, and only in worker prompts, not in session-start analysis); not visible in WorkerCard, not shown in UI when an agent is deployed
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Code review of agent-tools.ts will note: 'Good, memory_recall is implemented, finds similar tasks, returns a ToolResult.' A feature audit of worker execution will check: 'Can agents run tasks? Do they get results?' It won't ask: 'Do workers SHOW THE USER what precedent they're drawing from?' That transparency/narrative layer is invisible to domain auditing.
findings.impact: When a returning user sends an agent to 'analyze market entry for SEA region' on project 5, the agent silently recalls 'I analyzed SEA market entry before, got 4.2/5 approval' and uses that context. The user never sees this recall. They don't learn: 'This agent leveraged prior work.' They don't get confidence that the output is informed by precedent. The pattern accumulation is real but invisible, so users don't feel the moat growing.
findings.recommendation: In WorkerCard, add a 'Precedent' badge/section showing: 'This agent recalled 2 prior similar tasks (approval: 4.2★, 4.7★)' with expandable previews. Make it an affordance, not noise. If an agent has NO prior work, show 'First time on this task.' This visibility turns the invisible learning into narrative proof.

findings.title: Persona accuracy tracking is collected but not used to improve rehearsal persona selection
findings.evidence: src/stores/useAccuracyStore.ts (loadRatings, addRating, getPersonaAccuracySummary with bestAspects/worstAspects); accuracy_ratings table exists in Supabase; but src/lib/review-prompt.ts does not inject persona.accuracy or persona.worstAspects into the persona simulation prompt; PersonaFeedbackStep.tsx generates feedback without consulting prior accuracy data
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Feature audit of 'rehearsal' checks: Can users add personas? Can they rate accuracy? Is it stored? Yes to all. But cross-domain check: Does rehearsal round N use insights from accuracy ratings from prior rounds? Not checked. The storage layer and prompt layer are separate; both work, but the integration is missing.
findings.impact: User runs rehearsal with persona 'CEO demands ROI visibility' and later rates: 'Very accurate on financial scrutiny, but missed product strategy concerns.' This insight is recorded. In round 2 of the same project, the same persona is simulated again WITHOUT consulting this feedback. The persona makes the same strategic blind spot again. The user's effort to calibrate personas is wasted.
findings.recommendation: Pass persona.bestAspects and persona.worstAspects into the FEEDBACK_SYSTEM prompt in PersonaFeedbackStep.tsx. E.g., 'Based on prior rehearsals, this persona is sharp on financial details but tends to overlook market timing. Correct for that tendency here.' Also: when PersonaPoolModal suggests personas for a new project, rank by accuracy_score descending for personas already used in that org.

findings.title: Project cross-reference system exists but is low-visibility and not used for retrieval
findings.evidence: src/stores/useProjectStore.ts:39-44 (addRef method links projects via tool + itemId); src/app/project/page.tsx:656-672 (similar-project hint checks p.refs.length >= 2); but no full-text search for similar problem statements, no vector similarity, no 'export this insight to Project Y' affordance, refs are only internal links not discoverable from search
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A typical audit of 'project linking' will check: Can I tag one project with another? Is the link stored? Yes. But it won't ask: When I'm about to start Project 6 with a problem statement similar to Project 3, does the system FIND Project 3 and offer it? That requires cross-project semantic understanding, which is outside domain scope.
findings.impact: User completes 'competitor analysis for product launch' (Project 1), then 2 years later starts 'market entry strategy for new region' (Project 5). Both problems require competitive positioning analysis, but Project 5 starts from scratch. No system suggests: 'You've solved a similar problem before—your Project 1 competitive framework might apply.' The accumulated knowledge is siloed.
findings.recommendation: Add a pre-session suggestion: when user enters problemText in HeroFlow, compute semantic similarity against all prior projects' real_questions + surface_tasks. If match > 0.7, show: 'This resembles your [Project Name]. Resume from it? Or start fresh?' Also add an export: after completing a project, surface 'Transfer insights to another project' button that copies relevant decisions/assumptions.

findings.title: Session/voyage branching is feature-rich but old sessions are hard to re-enter
findings.evidence: src/stores/useProgressiveStore.ts:262-278 (forkBranch, switchBranch, restoreCheckpoint, navigateToCheckpoint fully implemented); VersionHistoryDrawer, VoyageChart UI support full branching; but no 'recent sessions' quick-access menu in workspace header, no breadcrumb showing 'Project > Session > Branch' context, sessions live in deep store state not easily searchable from UI
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A feature audit of 'voyage branching' will check: Can I fork? Restore? Switch branches? Yes. But UX audit won't catch: If I have 12 past sessions in this project, how do I find the one from 3 weeks ago where I explored scenario B? This is a navigation/discovery issue hidden behind a feature that works correctly.
findings.impact: Returning user wants to 'resume the risk-analysis branch from Project 3' but must: (1) Navigate to Project page, (2) Click Project 3, (3) Scroll workspace to find 'Open Past Session' option, (4) Find the right session in a list, (5) Click the version tree icon, (6) Find the right branch. Power users remember where they were but the UI makes it hard to re-enter.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Continue working' dropdown in workspace header showing: [Project Name] > [Last 3 sessions with timestamps] > [Active branch or most-recent branch]. One-click resume. Also: in project card on Projects page, show 'Continue: Branch name' instead of just 'Active' status.

findings.title: Learning health assessment exists but is not user-visible or actionable
findings.evidence: src/lib/learning-health.ts (assessLearningHealth computes signal_count, eval_coverage, override_trend, convergence_trend, learning_tier, recommendations); no UI displays this health check; assessLearningHealth is only called in tests and unused in main app
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Code review of learning-health.ts will show the function exists and is well-designed. But no audit will test: Where in the UI does the user see 'Your learning is at Tier 2, but eval_coverage is low'? The answer: nowhere. The feature is built but not wired to the interface.
findings.impact: The system can tell: 'Override trend is improving — your judgments are getting better' or 'Signal coverage is low — you're not evaluating assumptions enough.' But users never see this feedback. They miss opportunities to adjust their working style (e.g., 'I should be marking assumptions as verified more often').
findings.recommendation: Surface assessLearningHealth() in a user-visible 'Learning Insights' card on settings or project overview. Show tier, trend, and actionable recommendations. E.g., 'Your eval_coverage is 35% — trying to verify 1 more assumption per session would unlock Tier 3 bonuses.' Make it aspirational, not judgmental.

findings.title: No persistent 'user personas' or 'decision preferences' that carry across projects
findings.evidence: usePersonaStore.ts manages feedback personas (reviewers), not user personas; no useUserPreferencesStore; settings page allows user_name, user_role, user_seniority but these are static, not updated per decision; no 'I prefer more human steps than AI' or 'I always want 3+ reviewers' preference layer
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Settings audit checks: Can users enter their name/role? Yes. But cross-session pattern audit won't ask: Does the app remember that this user tends to prefer human judgment for strategic decisions and adjust initial role assignments? That requires a preferences layer that doesn't exist.
findings.impact: User on project 2 strongly prefers self-judgment (marked ~15 steps as 'human' instead of 'ai'). Project 3 starts with default 60% AI/40% human distribution again. No personalization based on observed preference. The user must re-teach the app their working style every project.
findings.recommendation: After each project completion, infer user preference from final role distribution: track ai_step_ratio, self_step_ratio, human_step_ratio. In next project, seed initial step assignments using this ratio. E.g., if user historically prefers 35% AI / 50% self / 15% human, bias the orchestrator toward that split (not mandatory, but default).

journeys.the_one_thing: The single most dangerous overlooked issue is the non-integration of judgment patterns into prompt contexts. ARGUS explicitly COLLECTS (useJudgmentStore.addJudgment), DISPLAYS (Project page "Your Judgment Patterns"), and ANALYZES (learning-health.ts override_trend) whether users override AI decisions and in which directions (AI→Human vs Human→AI shifts). But it does NOT FEED THIS BACK into the next session's AI prompt. As a result, a returning power user who has spent 4 projects training the app to understand their preference for human judgment on strategic decisions gets the same AI-forward default prompts on project 5. The moat promise—"사용할수록 똑똑해집니다"—is broken at the AI integration layer. The app learns about you and shows you a dashboard of what it learned. But the AI doesn't use that learning. This is a 1-line fix (pass userContext to buildInitialAnalysisPrompt) that would unlock the entire promised moat, but it's missing.

findings.title: Mobile bottom bar stacking collision and safe-area-inset miscalculation
findings.evidence: workspace/page.tsx:114 — pb-[calc(120px+env(safe-area-inset-bottom))] applies when hasWorkers, but LogbookDrawer (line 312) uses offset prop with hardcoded bottom-[56px] vs bottom-0, and WorkerDrawer (line 398-426) uses fixed bottom-0. On iPhone 14+ with notch/dynamic island, both drawers can appear simultaneously, obscuring content before safe area is properly accounted. ProgressiveLayout itself doesn't reserve space for QueryChatBar or NavigatorStrip in mobile view.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A mobile-focused domain audit would test individual components in isolation ("does the WorkerDrawer appear?", "does the LogbookDrawer dismiss?") and verify min-height: 44px buttons. A voyage-complete sweep shows the layering: user must navigate mobile bottom flows while managers are working (worker panel), while the logbook is open (offset bar), while quick-chat is collapsed below, with NavigatorStrip hiding behind lg:hidden. The three fixed-position layers don't communicate z-index order or safe-area stacking constraints.
findings.impact: On iPhone XS/11/12/13+ with safe area, user cannot see the last 2-3 lines of ProgressiveFlow content before the last worker is done. Last question in conversing phase may be obscured by LogbookDrawer + WorkerDrawer + OS home indicator. Only affects mobile; desktop avoids this because the right rail and left content coexist without overlap.
findings.recommendation: Implement a mobile-only layout context that tracks all 3 fixed bottom elements (Logbook + Worker + QuickChat) and programmatically calculates their cumulative height + safe-area-inset. Create a useMobileBottomReserve() hook returning { totalHeight, topPadding } and apply it as a single pb-[...] on the ProgressiveFlow wrapper. z-index should be Logbook (40) > Worker (41) > QuickChat (39) so stacking order is deterministic. Test on iPhone 12, 14, 15 Pro with home indicator and iOS keyboard visible.

findings.title: Long streaming outputs (worker results) unreadable on mobile due to narrow viewport and no word-wrap handling
findings.evidence: WorkerCard.tsx:108 renders overflow-y-auto on ResultModal with max-h-[85vh] but no max-width constraint. Modal is full-width on mobile (w-full) with sm:max-w-2xl on sm+ (line 89). Worker results can contain long code blocks, numbered lists, or table-like structures with no word-break or overflow-x handling. If a worker generates a 100+ word sentence or a code snippet, the text will overflow horizontally on phones without scroll. renderMd() function in line 115 doesn't mention word-break or hyphens CSS.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A text-rendering audit would check "does markdown render?" and "is contrast OK?" without actually viewing a real worker's response on a 390px-wide iPhone. The modal itself has responsive logic (sm:rounded-2xl vs rounded-t-2xl) but the *content* inside assumes a desktop or tablet width. The full voyage: user finishes answering questions, workers deploy, first worker returns 2000 tokens of analysis — user cannot read it on iPhone because the rendered markdown doesn't break lines at viewport bounds.
findings.impact: User cannot review long worker outputs on mobile without manually zooming in/out or rotating device. The primary mobile interaction — reading worker results to approve/reject — becomes unusable for any output >500 tokens. This blocks the entire approval step on mobile, forcing desktop fallback.
findings.recommendation: Add to ResultModal's flex-1 container: max-w-full with word-break: break-word, overflow-wrap: break-word, and hyphens: auto. Test renderMd() output by rendering a 1500+ token response (real worker output) in a 390px iframe. Verify code blocks use overflow-x-auto with scrollbar-hide. Consider wrapping long inline code with `<code>` tags using word-break: break-all internally, not at markdown layer.

findings.title: Question input (QuestionCard) loses focus and keyboard state on orientation change
findings.evidence: workspace/page.tsx doesn't have an onOrientationChange handler. QuestionCard textarea/input elements are uncontrolled on mobile when the user rotates from portrait to landscape. iOS Safari retains focus but Framer Motion animations (in QuestionCard) may remount, dropping the input value or caret position. No evidence of autoSave/lastValue recovery.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A UI audit tests form inputs under normal conditions. A full-voyage mobile audit exposes the real use case: user is reading a question on phone in portrait, starts to answer, rotates to landscape for more room — the input sometimes clears or loses focus. This is a "mobile moment" that doesn't occur on desktop.
findings.impact: If user types a long answer and rotates, they lose work. Causes frustration and increases bounce rate. Not critical (user can re-type) but undermines confidence in the app on mobile.
findings.recommendation: Add lastValue tracking to useProgressiveStore for each answer + checkpoint. On QuestionCard mount, check store and auto-fill. Ensure QuestionCard doesn't re-mount on orientation change — wrap in a stable key. Test on iOS Safari with split view and keyboard visible.

findings.title: VoyageChart SVG unresponsive to touch and too small on mobile
findings.evidence: VoyageChart.tsx:112 renders BranchMap inside max-h-[340px] overflow-y-auto. BranchMap.tsx:58-65 uses SVG with preserveAspectRatio='xMinYMin meet' and viewBox dynamically calculated but no touch-action or pointer-events tuning. SVG nodes (circle elements) have r=6-8px + 14px hit circles (line 121), which is adequate, but the overall SVG scales to 100% width on mobile. On a 390px phone, the entire voyage graph may compress to ~360px, making even the 14px hit areas feel small and hard to tap accurately.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A design audit checks contrast and touchability in isolation. A voyage audit realizes that the LogbookDrawer opens on mobile to show the waypoints and branch chart. The user then taps on the 'full chart' button in Logbook (line 105) to open VoyageChart in a modal. The modal is responsive but the SVG inside it doesn't account for the 390px width — nodes that are well-positioned on desktop (1200px+) become cramped clusters on phone.
findings.impact: User cannot easily fork branches or switch between courses on mobile because the chart is too compressed. Workaround: open desktop version. This is a core feature (branching) that becomes inaccessible on mobile.
findings.recommendation: Add a responsive SVG scaling rule: on mobile, bump the viewBox width proportionally or reflow nodes into a vertical tree instead of horizontal lanes (Phase 0 of ROADMAP mentions responsive layouts). Alternatively, increase the hit circle radius to 18px on mobile (detect via window.matchMedia('(max-width:768px)')), or add a pinch-to-zoom container around the SVG. Test on iPhone 12 by opening Logbook drawer → full chart modal → tapping different branch nodes.

findings.title: Worker approval step requires modal full-screen view, blocking quick approve/reject on mobile
findings.evidence: WorkerCard.tsx:67-144 ResultModal opens as a full-screen modal (max-h-[85vh] sm:max-h-[80vh]) to read the worker result. The approve/reject buttons are in the footer (lines 120-140). On mobile, the modal takes up the full screen, and the user must scroll to the footer to see the buttons. But the worker card itself (line 149+) shows inline approve/reject buttons when status=done. The modal is a duplicate surface for the same action.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A modal audit asks: 'does it open and close?' and 'are buttons accessible?'. A voyage audit tracks the real mobile workflow: worker returns result → user taps "read more" → modal opens → user reads → user must scroll down to footer → user taps approve → must wait for state update. On desktop, the same workflow is faster (sidebar shows result, buttons inline). The modal is a mobile UX fallback but becomes a friction point.
findings.impact: Approval workflow on mobile requires 3+ taps and scrolling, versus desktop's 1 tap. Users may skip reading long results and approve/reject without reviewing, reducing quality control on mobile.
findings.recommendation: On mobile, instead of a full-screen modal, use a bottom sheet (half-height) that shows the result summary with approve/reject buttons always visible at the bottom. Implement a sticky footer in the modal body so buttons are always accessible without scrolling. Or, inline the result text in the WorkerReportBlock itself without a modal, using collapsible details for full-text reading.

findings.title: Progressive streaming output (HeroFlow analyzing phase) doesn't account for mobile keyboard covering viewport
findings.evidence: workspace/page.tsx:295-620 HeroFlow (idle → assembling → analyzing → ready) renders streaming text in AnalysisCard components without any viewport observers. On mobile, when the user is typing in the initial textarea (line 365-370), the iOS keyboard covers ~50% of the viewport. After submission, the analyzing phase streams results in cards (lines 534-614), but there's no scroll-to-bottom or focus management. If the keyboard is still partially visible, the first-arriving results (real_question field) may render above the fold but the skeleton fields render below the keyboard, requiring manual scroll.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A component audit tests rendering logic. A voyage audit tests the real sequence: user opens workspace on mobile → sees HeroFlow → reads initial prompt → opens keyboard to type problem statement → types text → keyboard still visible → presses Start → analyzing phase begins, keyboard dismisses, but initial results render under the fold → user doesn't immediately see feedback that analysis started → user waits, unsure if the app is responsive.
findings.impact: On mobile, the first 2-3 seconds of the analyzing phase appear unresponsive because the results render off-screen. User may think the app hung or failed.
findings.recommendation: In HeroFlow's analyzing branch (line 502), use useEffect to dismiss the keyboard (blur the textarea) and scroll to the top of the results when analyzing phase starts. Add a Framer Motion scroll-into-view for the first AnalysisCard to ensure real_question field is visible within 500ms of first token arriving.

findings.title: Logbook drawer (mobile) max-h-[82vh] leaves no room for navigation if user has already scrolled the ProgressiveFlow
findings.evidence: Logbook.tsx:324 LogbookDrawer uses max-h-[82vh], which accounts for 18vh of top space (header + status bar). On iPhone 12 (812px height), 82vh = 666px max height. If the user has scrolled the ProgressiveFlow and the worker bar is visible at bottom (56px), the logbook drawer opening leaves only 666px for the waypoints list. With a header (52px) and footer hint (30px), only ~584px remains for scrolling waypoints. For voyages with 10+ waypoints, this is tight and the waypoint list becomes its own scroll container, which may confuse users (scroll inception).
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A drawer audit checks 'does it open and contain scrollable content?' without considering the cumulative scrolling layers. A voyage audit realizes: ProgressiveFlow is scrollable, LogbookDrawer overlays it with its own scroll, WorkerDrawer is below. User must manage 2-3 scroll contexts (main flow, logbook, worker panel). Each context has different content and different scroll speed expectations.
findings.impact: Waypoint navigation becomes cumbersome on long voyages. User must carefully scroll within the nested drawer without accidentally scrolling the background flow.
findings.recommendation: Reduce max-h to max-h-[75vh] to give more breathing room. Or, use a sticky header + footer pattern in the Logbook so the waypoint list fills available space. Test with a 15-waypoint voyage on iPhone to ensure scrolling is smooth and users don't accidentally interact with the background flow.

findings.title: Text input fields in modals (e.g., revision directive, team deploy) don't prevent keyboard z-index overlap
findings.evidence: ProgressiveFlow.tsx:2615-2624 textarea in the iteration/revision modal doesn't have any CSS to prevent keyboard from covering the input. On mobile, when the user focuses the textarea in the revision directive modal, the iOS keyboard slides up and may cover the textarea itself and the placeholder text, making it impossible to see what is being typed.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A form audit checks 'is the input focusable and does it accept text?' but doesn't simulate the mobile keyboard behavior. A mobile UX audit opens the modal on iPhone, taps the textarea, and immediately sees the keyboard covering the input.
findings.impact: User cannot see the text they are typing in modals on mobile, reducing confidence and increasing error rates.
findings.recommendation: Add CSS position: relative to the modal and use JavaScript to detect keyboard show event (iOS-specific: monitor visualViewport height changes). Scroll the modal up by keyboard height when a textarea gains focus, or use position: sticky on the textarea container to keep it above the keyboard. Test with the revision directive modal on iOS Safari with the keyboard visible.

findings.title: Persona settings panel (WorkerPanel.tsx) emoji and color pickers not optimized for touch
findings.evidence: WorkerPanel.tsx:160-167 emoji picker renders as 4 rows of 4 buttons (16 total) with no zoom or touch target enlargement. Each button is w-7 h-7 (28px), which is below the 44px minimum tap target. Color picker (line 191-197) shows 10 color buttons inline, each w-5 h-5 (20px) plus ring-offset, still below 44px. On mobile, these tiny buttons are hard to tap accurately.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: An accessibility audit would flag 'buttons < 44px minimum' but wouldn't test the real workflow: user is on mobile, wants to customize a team member's emoji, opens the WorkerPanel drawer, and tries to tap the emoji picker. The buttons are too small for their fingers.
findings.impact: User gives up on persona customization on mobile because the picker is too fiddly. Minor UX pain (not blocking) but reduces personalization engagement on mobile.
findings.recommendation: On mobile (window.matchMedia('(max-width:768px)')), enlarge emoji buttons to w-10 h-10 (40px) and reflow to 3 columns instead of 4 to keep the picker compact. Wrap color picker buttons in a touch-friendly 44px container. Or use a native color input if CSS support allows.

findings.title: NavigatorStrip (music insights panel) not hidden on mobile, overlaps with content
findings.evidence: NavigatorStrip.tsx:213-225 uses hidden lg:flex for the collapsed state. The expanded state also uses hidden lg:flex (line 229). However, if a user on a medium-sized tablet (md breakpoint = 768px, which is < lg 1024px) opens NavigatorStrip via a mobile-hidden button elsewhere, the component may render. More critically, NavigatorStrip is a sidebar toggle (not a drawer), so on mobile it would take up horizontal space if shown, conflicting with the main content.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A responsive audit checks 'is the component hidden on mobile?' but doesn't test the edge case of a user manually triggering the sidebar on a smaller device or a tablet at the md → lg boundary where the visual layout might break.
findings.impact: Minor. NavigatorStrip is hidden on mobile by default, so this is not a common issue. But if a user lands on the workspace page with an unusual viewport (e.g., landscape mode on iPhone, or a very tall narrow device), the sidebar may render and obscure content.
findings.recommendation: Add explicit md:hidden to NavigatorStrip even though it's lg:hidden, to ensure it's never visible on tablets or mobile in any orientation.

findings.title: No viewport meta tag enforcement for mobile — potential for user zoom causing layout shifts
findings.evidence: No explicit mention of viewport lock or zoom control in the codebase. If the app has user-scalable=no in the viewport meta tag, it violates accessibility guidelines. If user-scalable=yes (default), users can pinch-zoom, which may cause layout shifts in responsive components that don't account for zoomed text size (e.g., buttons with px-based padding may not scale).Workspace/page.tsx uses responsive classes like px-4 md:px-6, which scale with viewport but not with font zoom.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Accessibility audits check viewport settings but assume the app is designed to work at any zoom level. A mobile voyage audit reveals that some interactions (e.g., tiny emoji pickers, tight button spacing) are hard even at 100% zoom, and become impossible at 125% zoom.
findings.impact: Users with vision impairment who zoom to 125-150% may find buttons overlapping or text wrapping unexpectedly. Minor but affects inclusive design.
findings.recommendation: Ensure viewport meta tag allows zoom (user-scalable=yes) and test the app at 125% and 150% zoom on mobile. Audit all buttons and interactive elements to ensure they remain usable at zoomed sizes. This is a low-priority fix (accessibility concern, not usability blocker) but should be part of a mobile accessibility sweep.

journeys.lens: Mobile End-to-End Voyage UX — Can a Real Mobile User Complete a Full Voyage?
journeys.summary: ARGUS's mobile experience is structurally fragmented across three fixed-position bottom UI layers (LogbookDrawer, WorkerDrawer, QuickChatBar) that don't share layout information, causing content obscuring and safe-area miscalculation. The core voyage flow (HeroFlow → ProgressiveFlow → conversing → deploying workers → reviewing results) degrades significantly on mobile: streaming output text wraps incorrectly in modals, the VoyageChart branches are too small to tap reliably, and the worker approval workflow requires full-screen modals with scrolling. The approval step — the most critical interaction — becomes a 3+ tap, multi-scroll process on mobile versus 1 tap on desktop. Orientation changes lose form state, and keyboard management is absent from modals, making typing invisible. While individual components are responsive (buttons meet 44px minimum, breakpoints exist), their composition across the voyage reveals that mobile was never tested as an end-to-end scenario.
journeys.the_one_thing: The mobile bottom bar collision (LogbookDrawer + WorkerDrawer + safe-area-inset) simultaneously obscures the last 3 lines of the main ProgressiveFlow content while forcing the user to manage stacked scroll contexts, breaking the core interaction flow of conversing-with-questions and reviewing-worker-results. This is the single most dangerous overlooked issue because it's not a polish problem — it's an architecture problem that makes the entire mobile voyage experience feel broken, despite the code being "responsive" (individual widths adapt, buttons scale, etc.). A user on mobile cannot answer the final question or see if workers are done because the drawer layers bury the content underneath.

adversary.lens: PRODUCT-THESIS PREMORTEM: "Why Argus Failed at Scale (12 Months Later)"
adversary.summary: Argus is architecturally sophisticated and philosophically coherent, with Phase 0-2 of its roadmap mostly implemented. However, the product rests on three unproven assumptions about human behavior that the code reveals are not yet validated: (1) that "thinking before doing" creates durable behavior change, not a one-time novelty; (2) that a metaphor-heavy brand can sustain engagement across non-specialist audiences without becoming friction; and (3) that *meta-reflection itself* (the "5th moment") is a retention hook when the actual outputs (Prompt Chain, Agent Spec) are static markdown—nearly invisible in daily tools. The real failure mode is not execution or design quality, but a fundamental mismatch between the product's value thesis (judgment structuring) and the actual value moments users experience (getting a usable output, fast). The voyage metaphor and the "thinking before acting" philosophy are internally coherent but operate at a level of abstraction that may never translate to repeated opens.

findings.title: The Output-to-Retention Gap: Markdown Artifacts Don't Drive Repeat Use
findings.evidence: src/lib/project-brief.ts, src/lib/agent-spec.ts, src/components/ui/OutputSelector.tsx (all 4 outputs are static markdown generated once). Analytics suggests 'output_generated' event tracking but no 'output_copy' → 'repeat_question' funnel. The philosophy promises 'Project Brief / Prompt Chain / Agent Spec / Execution Checklist' as the payoff (§5 Ithaca), but these are one-time artifacts, not living documents users refine.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A domain audit would validate that outputs are *correct* and *well-formatted*. It wouldn't ask: 'Do users actually reference these outputs 2 weeks later?' or 'Does generating the same output again feel worth the effort?' The product thesis assumes outputs are inherently valuable, but execution audits only verify that outputs exist, not that they drive behavior change.
findings.impact: Users complete a voyage once, download a Prompt Chain, and never return because the artifact is stale 3 days later (code changed, requirements shifted, team composition changed). The product becomes a 'one-off tool' like a PDF generator, not a 'coach you return to.' Viral/word-of-mouth is impossible because 'generate a Prompt Chain for my project' is not a repeatable ask.
findings.recommendation: Before scaling, validate: (1) What % of users who generate outputs actually *use* them in real work? (2) Do users generate outputs for the same project 2+ times? (3) If not, what would make them? (a) Live output refinement? (b) 'Share decision log with team' feedback loop? (c) Templating from past projects? Test at least one of these with 20-30 power users before claiming outputs are a retention hook.

findings.title: Meta-Reflection (5th Moment) Is Claimed as Retention but Has Zero Incentive
findings.evidence: src/components/ui/OutputSelector.tsx defines meta_reflection with three questions (understanding_change, surprising_discovery, next_time_differently), and philosophy (§10, moment 5) claims this is 'meta-cognitive asset accumulation.' But (1) reflection is *optional* ('부드럽게 제안한다'), (2) there's no UI showing accumulated reflections, (3) no cross-project learning feature, (4) no reminder/prompt to revisit them. Code: 'codaSaved ? L('업데이트') : L('성찰 저장')' suggests saving is secondary, not core flow.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A UX audit would verify that the reflection UI is clear and accessible. It wouldn't ask: 'Why would I fill this out?' or 'What happens to my reflection after I save it?' The product claims reflection compounds across sessions, but there's no mechanism to surface past reflections, no spaced repetition, no 'look how much you've learned' dashboard. A feature that's 'optional' and 'invisible' is effectively not there.
findings.impact: Reflection data is captured but unutilized, creating the illusion of a learning loop without the mechanism. Users who *do* engage in reflection get no signal of progress or payoff, so they don't repeat. The philosophy's promise ('메타 보정의 실제 적용') remains purely aspirational.
findings.recommendation: Either: (1) Delete the reflection feature and be honest that outputs are the deliverable, or (2) Redesign reflection as a *required* microinteraction (2-3 sentences, not 3 questions) + surface it in the project dashboard as 'Your growth' or 'What you've learned.' If reflection is genuinely valuable, make it visible and rewarding, not a hidden checkbox.

findings.title: The Judgment-Learning Loop (Phase 4) Is Not Implemented, Yet Is Core to the Moat
findings.evidence: ROADMAP.md §4 defines 'Self-Improving System' (Phase 4) with detailed BinaryEval framework. src/lib/eval-engine.ts exists and implements REFRAME_EVALS, but these evals are *recorded* not *acted on*. No code found that: (1) aggregates eval results across users, (2) adjusts system prompts based on performance, (3) detects 'high pass rate but low utility' patterns (anti-gaming), or (4) maintains PromptVersions with mutation tracking. Eval data is collected but never feeds back to improve the product.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A correctness audit verifies that eval recording logic is correct. It doesn't interrogate: 'Are evals actually improving the system?' The philosophy (§1.5) claims 'Argus자체가 가치 있는 산출물이다'—the learning is the product. But the learning infrastructure is half-built: data is collected but the feedback loop is closed.
findings.impact: All the architectural sophistication (context-chain, reframing-strategy, eval-engine) is wasted because there's no force moving the system forward. Every user gets the same system prompts as every other user in 2024 as in 2026. The product has no *defensibility*—there's no accumulated intelligence that makes Argus better than ChatGPT + a good template. The real moat (learning from usage patterns) is incomplete, so the product is vulnerable to OpenAI releasing a 'structured thinking mode' in GPT-5.
findings.recommendation: Prioritize Phase 4 implementation: (1) Add mutation hypothesis tracking to all SYSTEM_PROMPT changes. (2) Aggregate eval results weekly to detect winning strategy + assumption patterns. (3) A/B test 2-3 prompt mutations with new users monthly (opt-in). (4) Publish 'what we learned this month' as a signal that the system is improving. Without this, Phase 0-2 sophistication is just technical debt.

findings.title: The 'Just ChatGPT' Threat Is Existential But Not Addressed in Code
findings.evidence: Philosophy (§7.3): 'Argus의 진짜 경쟁자는 "그냥 바로 ChatGPT에 물어보기"' — the admission itself. But the product has zero *forced friction* that makes this impossible. A user can skip 항로 재설정 and go straight to 'write a prompt' (no UX blocker). The voyage metaphor is entirely *post-hoc justification* after a better idea exists. Code shows no aggressive onboarding that makes the 'structured thinking' habit stick (no daily prompts, no project templates, no 'you skipped the thinking step, here's why that failed' learning).
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A domain audit looks at competition positioning and messaging clarity, which are strong.
