It wouldn't ask: 'If a user has ChatGPT open in another tab, why would they type here instead?' Or: 'What makes the thinking discipline *stick*?' The product assumes the value is obvious ('better outputs'), but the mechanism for *converting* users from 'thinking is optional' to 'thinking is how I work' is absent.
findings.impact: Viral adoption is impossible because the product's value only reveals itself to users who already believe 'thinking before acting matters.' For those users, Argus is great. For the 99% who would be helped by structured thinking but don't self-identify as needing it, the pitch ('think before you recast') sounds like overhead, not leverage. The product will plateau at 'enthusiasts who like the philosophy' (5-10% TAM) and never cross to mainstream (which requires either obsessive UX or network effects).
findings.recommendation: Validate the core assumption with real data: What % of users who *do* complete a full voyage report better outcomes than if they'd just asked ChatGPT? If >60% yes, then invest in habit formation (daily challenges, templates, team mode). If <40% yes, the philosophy is wrong, not the execution, and no UX polish will help.

findings.title: The Voyage Metaphor Has a Half-Life — Beginners Might Understand It, But It Becomes Baggage
findings.evidence: Philosophy (§4.1) correctly warns: '비유를 학습해야 제품을 쓸 수 있다면 그 메타포는 실패한 것이다.' But the actual product *is* the metaphor: pages are named '항로 재설정' (not 'Problem Reframing'), UI labels use voyage language ('선원 배치', '리허설', '항로 수정'), and the landing page is an elaborate 'Act 1 Voyage' narrative. Even the org structure in codebase mirrors the metaphor (components/landing/voyage, components/workspace/progressive/Logbook, etc.). For new users, this is charming. For power users repeating projects 5 times, it's consistently indirect language overhead.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A UX/language audit would verify that metaphor language is consistent and not confusing—a pass. But it wouldn't measure *cognitive load over time*. After 10 projects, 'Set the Heading' might feel quaint compared to 'Define the Problem.' The philosophy says '업무명과 항상 병기' (always pair metaphor with task name), but in many places, only the metaphor appears in button labels and headings.
findings.impact: Power users (who would bring word-of-mouth credibility) encounter friction: they have to constantly contextualize voyage language in their real work. This is not a dealbreaker, but it prevents word-of-mouth ('this tool is amazing, try it') because the metaphor doesn't compress: you can't explain Argus in 30 seconds without spending 10 seconds on the voyage theme. Tools that grow via word-of-mouth are usually *concept-simple* (Notion: 'one database for all your content'). Argus is *metaphorically rich* but *conceptually opaque*.
findings.recommendation: A/B test: Landing page + onboarding flow with metaphor vs. without (same functionality, stripped language). If metaphor-free version has higher LTV or longer session times, consider a 'classic mode' toggle or a slower introduction of voyage language (only on landing, then fade to functional names in the app).

findings.title: No Pathways for Teams or Collaborative Judgment — Product Is Built for Solo Decision-Makers
findings.evidence: Code architecture: all stores (useReframeStore, useRecastStore, usePersonaStore) are single-user, localStorage-first + Supabase async. Philosophy (§2.2) mentions 'Team Specification' and 'Steering Documents' (from SDD), but these are aspirations, not implemented. The 'Project' model has no team_members, no permission model, no 'share decision log' feature. README mentions 'Claude Code 플러그인' for team mode (/argus:team), but this is a separate product.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A data model audit would verify schema correctness for individual projects. It wouldn't ask: 'Is the product usable by teams?' or 'Do strategic decisions actually happen solo?' Real strategic decisions (go/no-go decisions, product direction, hire/fire calls) are *organizational*, not individual. A team's collective judgment is what matters, but the product has no mechanism for team deliberation, only individual reflection.
findings.impact: TAM is limited to solo decision-makers (individual strategists, consultants, solopreneurs) and never expands to teams/orgs. Enterprises are permanently out of reach because you can't govern which decisions are made, who made them, or what the org's collective judgment was. Word-of-mouth from a consultant to their client team is blocked because the client has no shared workspace to continue the deliberation.
findings.recommendation: Don't build team features yet—validate if solo use is actually the blocker to retention. If 50%+ of users who complete a voyage share the output with 1+ colleague and ask for feedback, *then* justify team mode. If <10% share and seek feedback, the philosophy is correct (individual thinking is the lever) and team features would be cargo-cult feature-creep.

findings.title: Progressive Flow Branching UI Is Sophisticated but Solves No Retention Problem
findings.evidence: ProgressiveFlow.tsx (~2670 lines) implements branching, checkpoints, version history, course-line colors, and voyage checkpoints. VoyageChart shows a git-graph-style visualization of iterations. This is high-craft engineering. But the UX question is: *Why would users branch?* If a user completes a full voyage (항로 재설정 → 선원 배치 → 리허설 → 항로 수정 → Ithaca), what reason do they have to fork and retry? The philosophy doesn't explain a use case. The code shows branching as possible ('프리모템 후 대안 항로 검토'), but not as a *driver of repeated use*.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A complexity audit would ask if branching UX is clear and performant—likely yes. But it wouldn't ask: 'Is this feature solving a real problem or is it YAGNI?' The product team built branching (possibly after /blindspot or /rehearse feedback about 'what if we try a different angle?'), but there's no data showing that users who branch are more retained than users who converge once and leave.
findings.impact: Branching is a feature that justifies the architecture (version trees, checkpoints, voyage graphs) but doesn't justify the product. It's architectural sophistication masquerading as user value. If users never branch, it's technical debt. If users do branch frequently, the original prompt should have been clearer, not branching-friendly.
findings.recommendation: Instrument: 'branching_event' → if <5% of voyages spawn 2+ branches, delete the branching UI and simplify to linear flow. If >15% of voyages branch, investigate: do branchers have longer LTV? If yes, understand why and amplify the pattern. If no, branching is a red herring.

findings.title: The API/Integration Strategy Is Unclear — Outputs Are Markdown, Not Machine-Readable Systems
findings.evidence: Agent Spec is generated as YAML (src/lib/agent-spec.ts), but there's no evidence it's used by real LangGraph/CrewAI implementations. The README claims 'Agent Spec — LangGraph/CrewAI 구현의 출발점' (starting point), but 'starting point' could mean 'someone manually reads it and codes.' There's no auto-compilation to executable LangGraph specs. The Prompt Chain is plain text, not a structured prompt object with parameterization. This makes the 4 outputs look integrated but they're actually disconnected manuscripts.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A correctness audit verifies that YAML is valid and markdown renders cleanly. It wouldn't test: 'Can I feed this Agent Spec directly into LangGraph.compile()?'  or 'Does the Prompt Chain actually work when pasted into Claude?' (likely yes for Prompt Chain, but probably needs manual tweaking for Agent Spec).
findings.impact: The outputs feel like the 'full solution' (Project Brief, Prompt Chain, Agent Spec, Checklist) but they're actually 4 separate documents that require manual bridging to become a real system. This breaks the 'bridge between judgment and execution' promise. If outputs required 20% manual work to use, that's 80% leverage. If they require 50%+ manual work, they're just fancy documentation.
findings.recommendation: Before 2.0: Validate with 10 users: 'Here's your Agent Spec. How long to get it running in LangGraph?' If median is >30 min, the output is premature abstraction. If median is <10 min, it's probably not detailed enough for real use.

findings.title: The 'Think Before You Recast' Thesis Is Aspirational, Not Validated Under Pressure
findings.evidence: The philosophy (§1, §7.3) is built on one assumption: users *want to think better* and *will spend time structuring judgment before acting*. But there's no evidence that (1) a 10-minute structured thinking session *actually produces measurably better results* than 5 minutes with ChatGPT, or (2) users perceive the value *during* the voyage, not in retrospect. The 5 moments (§10) are what *Argus believes* should happen, not what necessarily does. Code has no A/B test infrastructure for validating the core thesis.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A domain audit would verify that the app delivers the 5 moments via the UX. But it wouldn't ask: 'Are these moments actually valuable?' Product philosophers describe the experience they want users to have, but users might experience something different: time-consuming form-filling, jargon overhead, and a markdown file they'll never use.
findings.impact: This is the existential risk. If the 5 moments don't actually lead to better decisions or faster execution, the product is philosophically beautiful but commercially invalid. Users might feel smart while using Argus ('I'm thinking deeply!') but then never return because the outputs didn't unlock value they couldn't get elsewhere.
findings.recommendation: Run a 4-week quasi-experiment with 30 paid power users (must complete 2+ full voyages). Cohort A: Argus full flow (all 5 moments). Cohort B: Argus express (skip 항로 수정, go straight to Ithaca). Measure: (1) Do Cohort A outputs actually get used more? (2) Do Cohort A users return for a 2nd voyage at higher rates? If no significant diff, the philosophy is wrong, not the execution.

adversary.the_one_thing: The product's deepest blind spot is treating *thinking* as the output, not as a mechanism for better *doing*. The philosophy brilliantly frames judgment-structuring as the valuable activity (meta-reflection, assumption testing, risk rehearsal), but the code reveals that the actual output to users is static markdown artifacts (Project Brief, Prompt Chain, Agent Spec). These artifacts are one-time use. Once you download the Prompt Chain, there's no reason to ever return to Argus unless you have a *different* decision to make. But most people don't make strategic decisions daily—they make them quarterly or yearly. So Argus becomes a tool you use once a quarter, not a habit. The philosophy assumes that *doing the thinking* is rewarding enough to come back, but in reality, users are reward-seeking: they want outcomes, not process. The missing retention hook is not better outputs or team features—it's a genuine reason to return to Argus within 7 days. That might be 'refine your past decision based on real feedback' (live artifact versioning), or 'compare 3 decisions you've made' (cross-project learning), or 'daily dose of judgment-testing' (challenges/prompts). But none of those exist, so the product is built for a motivation (love of judgment discipline) that most users don't have.

adversary.lens: COMPETITIVE TEARDOWN: Capability Gaps vs. Positioned Competitors (BMAD, RIPER-5, SDD, Claude Code Plan Mode, CrewAI/LangGraph, autoresearch)
adversary.summary: Argus positions itself as "the decision engine before all execution tools," occupying a unique anti-ChatGPT niche: structured judgment before LLM agenticide. However, a comparative teardown against BMAD-METHOD, SDD, Claude Code Plan Mode, CrewAI, and autoresearch reveals that Argus lacks six critical capabilities that competitors have already solved: (1) real-time agent orchestration & execution tracking (BMAD, CrewAI have this; Argus outputs static markdown); (2) automated self-improvement loops at system-prompt level (autoresearch does this; Phase 4 is roadmapped but unbuilt); (3) bidirectional specification-to-execution binding (SDD's core; Argus breaks after "Ithaca" outputs); (4) sub-second planning in IDE/embedded context (Claude Code Plan Mode ships this; Argus is web-only); (5) heterogeneous agent team instantiation (BMAD's 3-agent fan-out; Argus hard-codes persona roles); (6) cross-project pattern mining & network effects (Phase 6 roadmapped; competitors ship with user-pooled intelligence). Most dangerously, Argus's "judgment before execution" thesis is undercut by its inability to instrument *actual execution* — it has no feedback loop from deployed decisions back into the judgment engine, making learned patterns asymptotic and unvalidated.

findings.title: No Real-Time Execution Instrumentation — Broken Feedback Loop
findings.evidence: ROADMAP.md §3 'Execution Checklist 2.0' is static markdown; no LiveChecklist, no webhook capture, no decision-outcome binding. BMAD Phase 3 & CrewAI's 450M+ workflows/month both include execution logging. Argus's Agent Spec outputs LangGraph-compatible YAML (src/lib/agent-spec.ts), but has zero instrumentation to capture what *actually executed* — no way to know if a Persona's predicted concern was real, if a critical assumption held, or if a step failed.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Domain audits look at output quality (brief accuracy, persona fidelity, risk classification). They don't see the *structural missing piece*: validation data. In BMAD & autoresearch, every execution feeds back into the judgment loop (new evals, strategy weights). Argus has evals defined (eval-engine.ts, Phase 1 binary evals) but *no source of truth for what happened downstream*. The audit sees 'evals exist' and moves on; it misses that they're measured against *user perception* not *reality*.
findings.impact: Users can't trust Argus recommendations because they're not learning from outcomes. A Persona's 'approval_conditions' might be dead wrong, but Argus has no mechanism to discover this. Phase 1 evals measure 'did the user accept the reframing?' not 'did the reframing predict the actual problem?' This asymptotes Argus's value — it becomes a structure machine, not a learning engine.
findings.recommendation: Add a PostExecutionHook API: allow CrewAI/LangGraph/Claude Code tasks to POST back `{ decision_id, outcome, metrics, assumption_status }`. Wire this to eval-engine so Phase 1 'question_accepted' eval can be validated against real-world signal. This requires: (1) Supabase table for execution outcomes, (2) lightweight webhook receiver in src/app/api, (3) callback in exported Agent Spec, (4) refactored evals to weight 'user said OK' vs 'user said OK *and outcome was good*'.

findings.title: Static Output Artifacts Block Execution Binding (SDD Bidirectionality Gap)
findings.evidence: Argus outputs 4 formats: Project Brief (markdown), Prompt Chain (markdown), Agent Spec (YAML), Checklist (markdown). SDD (github.com/github/spec-kit) treats specs as *executable* — spec → plan → code → live system → spec evolution. Argus 'Ithaca' is *terminal* output (src/components/workspace/SynthesizeStep.tsx, no 'return to Recast if assumptions fail' loop). ROADMAP Phase 5 says 'Prompt Chain 2.0 with context comments' but this is still copy-paste. SDD's 'Steering Documents' stay in the repo; they co-evolve with code. Argus artifacts stay in browser localStorage/Supabase.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Output audits check: is the brief clear? Are the personas well-defined? Do checklists have enough detail? Yes. What they miss: can a deployed system *query* the decision rationale? Can a failed assumption trigger a re-Recast? Can a code PR reference the judgment that authorized it? SDD does all three; Argus does none. The audit never looks at how the decision artifact *lives* after generation.
findings.impact: Argus is a one-way mirror: it consumes ambiguous human intent, outputs crisp artifacts, then exits. Real-world decisions mutate (scope changes, market shifts, team composition evolves). SDD-style systems stay versioned and co-evolved with execution. Argus artifacts become stale within weeks because there's no mechanism to keep them in sync with reality.
findings.recommendation: Build a DecisionRegistry: (1) Export all outputs to a GitHub branch (.argus/ folder with YAML decision records, executable as Steering Docs). (2) Add DecisionLink fields to LLM prompts ('decision_id: 8f2a...' in Agent Spec, Prompt Chain comments). (3) Implement 'Assumption Failed' webhook handler that auto-triggers Refine step. (4) Wire Supabase's 'decision.status' to track 'active'/'obsolete'/'superseded'. This mirrors SDD's specification-as-living-artifact.

findings.title: No Heterogeneous Agent Team Instantiation — Locked Role Set
findings.evidence: BMAD docs (docs.bmad-method.org) describe dynamic agent selection: Analyst, Project Manager, Architect, and domain-specific reviewers (Go-to-market, Technical Feasibility, Change Management) chosen per task. ROADMAP Phase 2 §'Multi-Lens Recasting' designs 3-lens parallel review (Skeptic, Optimizer, Domain), but src/lib implements only fixed personas (PersonaStore has ~12 hardcoded personas). Phase 2 'selectDomainReviewer()' is designed but unbuilt. Instead, all Rehearsal runs against user-selected stakeholders, not task-optimized reviewers.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A quality audit sees: personas are realistic, feedback is credible. It doesn't see the *lost opportunity*: if the task is 'market entry decision,' why ask the CTO (fixed persona) instead of a Go-to-Market specialist auto-summoned by task type? BMAD's capability is 'agents are selected to fit the problem'; Argus's model is 'user curates stakeholders.' The audit confirms the latter works but misses that the former would be better.
findings.impact: Argus can't deep-dive multifaceted problems. A product relaunch needs simultaneous legal, market, execution, and change-management perspectives — but if the user hasn't pre-enrolled these personas, Argus falls back to generic stakeholders. BMAD would spawn them automatically. This limits Argus to teams that already know their stakeholder map.
findings.recommendation: Implement selectReviewerTeam(taskDescription, existingPersonas) → AgentTeam. (1) Parse task via Claude to extract domain signals ('market', 'legal', 'technical', 'change', 'customer'). (2) Map to Persona archetypes: if domain includes 'legal' and user has no lawyer persona, auto-create from template. (3) Use CrewAI-style agent definition to spawn lightweight 'domain_expert' variants. (4) Run 3-lens parallel review with mixed fixed + dynamic team. (5) Store dynamic persona configs in Supabase so patterns are reusable across sessions.

findings.title: No Autonomous Prompt Mutation & Pass-Rate Learning (autoresearch Gap)
findings.evidence: ROADMAP Phase 4 ('Self-Improving System') is a complete design: BinaryEval framework, PromptVersion tracking, autonomous mutation loop, git-backed changelog. src/lib/eval-engine.ts implements binary evals (6 defined, correct count per autoresearch rules). src/lib/prompt-mutation.ts exists. BUT: there is *zero automation*. No CI loop that runs 50+ sessions, measures pass rates, proposes mutations, tests them, commits winners. autoresearch-skill (GitHub uditgoenka/autoresearch) ships this live — define metric, it runs overnight, you wake up to improved prompts. Argus's evals are *measured* (stored in localStorage/Supabase) but never *acted upon*.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: An audit can see evals are well-designed, signal recording works (signal-recorder.ts), storage is sound. It can't see the *missing runtime*: there is no PromptVersionManager that wakes up, reads eval history, proposes 'clarify instructions more specifically' mutations, tests them, and commits the good ones. The code exists to *define* mutations; none exists to *execute* them.
findings.impact: Argus can't learn from use. Every user iteration is fresh; Argus never gets better as a product because there's no overnight eval harness saying 'decompose strategy X has 62% pass rate vs. 48% for Y; flip the default.' This blocks Phase 1 Adaptive Decompose (adaptive strategy selection based on interview signals) from ever activating — without production eval data, there's nothing to adapt *to*.
findings.recommendation: Build PromptEvolutionDaemon: (1) Collect 50+ eval results (per autoresearch rules, minimum sample size). (2) Weekly cron job runs PromptMutationProposer: parses eval failures, generates 2-3 hypotheses (e.g., 'reframed_question instructions lack specificity'), writes mutations to prompt_versions table. (3) For each mutation, spawn 3-5 parallel test sessions (via Claude API batch mode to minimize cost). (4) Measure mutation's pass rate against baseline. (5) If win > 5% and no regression on other evals, auto-commit with changelog. (6) Tag production prompt with latest winning version. This requires: new Supabase tables (prompt_versions, eval_runs), weekly cron endpoint, mutation template library.

findings.title: IDE/Embedded Integration Only as Plugin — Not First-Class in Claude Code
findings.evidence: Argus web app is hosted at argus.voyage (Next.js, full workspace UI). Claude Code integration is via argus-plugin-v2 (src/app/api/slack & email hooks, but main decision flow happens in web browser). Compare: Claude Code Plan Mode (cursor.com/blog/plan-mode) is *native* — Shift+Tab in Agent, plan appears inline. SDD is GitHub-native (spec-kit templates integrate into repos). CrewAI & LangGraph are Python libraries (pip install, use anywhere). Argus forces detour: open browser, enter question, export, paste into code. This is 'web app integrating with IDE' not 'IDE-native judgment tool.'
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Audit checks: does plugin work? Can you run /argus:sail? Yes, it works. The audit doesn't measure *friction*: context switch from IDE to browser, re-entering context (what am I trying to decide?), pasting artifact back. Claude Code Plan Mode reduces this to 2 seconds. Argus's plugin (README.md) is a *wrapper* that calls the web app, not a first-class implementation.
findings.impact: Argus's adoption bottleneck is not quality but friction. A Claude Code user with a live codebase question sees '/argus:sail...' takes 30 seconds of context switching vs. planning inline (native plan mode) taking 5 seconds. Network effects are strangled — users won't pull Argus into daily IDE workflow if it requires a browser tab.
findings.recommendation: Port core judgment engine to TypeScript library (separate from web UI): @argus/judgment-engine (exports ReframeEngine, RecastEngine, RehearseEngine as classes). Rewrite plugin-v2 to instantiate these locally (vs. calling web API). This requires: (1) Extract src/lib prompts & context builders into @argus/core package (no React deps). (2) Publish to npm. (3) Rewrite argus-plugin-v2 to use it (index.ts imports ReframeEngine, binds to /argus:sail). (4) Make plan-mode-like inline results possible (5-10 lines of JSON, not full HTML). This mirrors how Cursor Plan Mode is *native* to the IDE.

findings.title: No Cross-Project Pattern Mining & Intelligence Pooling (Phase 6 Unbuilt)
findings.evidence: ROADMAP Phase 6 (§'Cross-User Intelligence') describes reframing_patterns table with anonymized interview_signal_hash + strategy + pass_rate. Goals: new users inherit insights from 47 similar prior projects. BUT: (1) no multi-user Supabase setup (only personal projects in current schema); (2) no privacy model for sharing judgment patterns; (3) no aggregation pipeline; (4) no UI to surface 'experts in your space have tried X strategy with 78% success'. Competitors: BMAD's docs mention 'standardized workflows' (reused across orgs); CrewAI does 450M workflows/month with 60% Fortune 500 adoption — they're pooling patterns. Argus remains siloed.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A single-player audit sees: does Argus work for one user doing one project? Yes. It doesn't check: does it get *exponentially better* with more users? That's Phase 6, and it's unbuilt. The audit never compares against CrewAI's 'Enterprise Crews' (shared agent templates across teams) or BMAD's standardized workflows (reusable across orgs).
findings.impact: Argus has no network effects. A 1000-person user base yields no advantage over 10-person base (vs. competitors, where user count = better default strategies). This blocks exponential adoption. New users start from zero context, unable to benefit from thousands of prior decisions.
findings.recommendation: Implement PartternPool: (1) Create multi-tenant schema (projects.org_id, decisions.org_id; anonymized cross-org views). (2) Weekly aggregation: hash interview_signal combinations, compute strategy_success_rate by org-type (startup, enterprise, nonprofit). (3) UI card on Reframe step: 'Companies like yours chose [strategy] 78% of the time. Consider?' (4) Add PatternExplorer page (project/patterns) showing your org's reframing history + anonymous peers. (5) Privacy: no org names in cross-org views, only aggregates. This requires schema migration, analytics pipeline (maybe BigQuery), and new UI components.

findings.title: BMAD's Simultaneous Multi-Agent Review Unprepared — Debate Engine Incomplete
findings.evidence: ROADMAP Phase 2 designs parallel 3-lens review (Skeptic, Optimizer, Domain agent). Parallel execution requires coordination: conflict detection, consensus-seeking, fallback voting. src/lib/debate-engine.ts exists (imports in RehearseStep.tsx) but is lightweight — focuses on persona debate within a *single* rehearsal, not *parallel agent output merging*. BMAD's multi-agent pattern includes explicit conflict resolution: if Agent-A says 'proceed' and Agent-B says 'halt', the system surfaces this as actionable tension (not one agent overriding the other). Argus Rehearsal runs sequentially through user-selected personas; merging agent outputs is a stub.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Audit checks: are personas credible? Does debate output exist? Yes. It doesn't check: what happens when Skeptic says 'critical gap' and Optimizer says 'redundant step'? Is that a conflict worth surfacing? Argus's current code threads all feedback together (likely in a list). BMAD's pattern is explicit: conflicts are *structured data* (side_a, side_b, tie-breaking_condition) so the user can decide. Audit misses this distinction.
findings.impact: High-stakes decisions fail silently. If two personas contradict, Argus can't reliably surface this as a red flag requiring executive decision. It gets lost in the noise of feedback lists. BMAD surfaces contradictions as first-class citizens (user can see 'unresolved tension: Victor vs Arthur').
findings.recommendation: Enhance debate-engine: (1) Implement DebateFrame type: { side_a: { agent, position, reasoning }, side_b: { agent, position, reasoning }, tie_breaking_condition: string }. (2) In Phase 2 multi-lens review, run LLM conflict detector after 3 agents report: 'do these outputs contradict on any dimension?' (3) Surface contradictions in RehearseStep as 'Team Contradiction' card (visual prominence). (4) Add UI button: 'Resolve: I side with [agent]' → records user judgment → feeds into Refine loop (re-Recast with user's tie-breaker). (5) Store contradictions in decision_artifacts table for learning.

findings.title: No Live Checklist State Sync or Step-Conditional Branching
findings.evidence: Argus Checklist is static markdown export (output from Agent Spec). ROADMAP Phase 5 says 'Execution Checklist 2.0: Supabase-backed, real-time updates, assumption failure triggers alerts.' But implementation is absent. src/stores has no ChecklistStore or LiveTask tracking. Compare: GitHub Projects (SDD-native) syncs checklist state with PRs/issues in realtime. CrewAI Crews have built-in task status (pending, running, completed, failed). Argus outputs frozen checklist; execution is out of band.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Audit sees: checklist format is clear, checkpoints are well-defined. Doesn't see: checklist state is *never written back* to Argus. If step 2 fails (assumption turns out false), Argus doesn't know, can't auto-trigger Refine. Checklist exists in GitHub Issues or Slack, not in Argus.
findings.impact: Incomplete feedback loop. A failed assumption or blocked checkpoint in execution never cycles back to the judgment engine. The decision decays: checkpoints are checked in Jira, but Argus is unaware.
findings.recommendation: Build ChecklistSync: (1) Add ChecklistStore with task records (decision_id, step_id, status, completed_by, note, assumption_verified). (2) Export checklist with embedded webhook URLs or Slack thread (so team can click 'Complete' / 'Assumption Failed' inline). (3) On webhook arrival, update ChecklistStore + auto-trigger Refine if any assumption marked 'failed' or critical checkpoint blocked >1 hour. (4) UI: add ChecklistStatus page (project/decision/:id/checklist) showing live task state.

findings.title: Persona Accuracy Learning Siloed — No Cross-Session Pattern Transfer
findings.evidence: ROADMAP Phase 3 ('Rehearsal Intelligence') designs PersonaBehaviorModel: accuracy_by_aspect, blind_spots, calibration_notes. src/stores/usePersonaStore.ts has accuracy_ratings array. But there's no mechanism to (1) extract patterns like 'this CEO always underestimates technical risk by 30%' and auto-apply to next project, (2) detect 'blind_spots' (things this persona consistently misses), (3) pool cross-project persona data (same person persona used in 3 projects — do patterns cluster?). Instead, each decision re-simulates personas from scratch, inheriting zero prior feedback.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Audit checks: are accuracy ratings collected? Is feedback stored? Yes (PersonaFeedbackStep.tsx records them). Doesn't check: are these ratings *learned from*? That code doesn't exist. Audit sees data collection as complete, not realizing there's no inference layer on top of it.
findings.impact: Personas don't improve. A CFO persona that's wrong in project A is equally wrong in project B (user must re-calibrate manually). Network effect is broken — personas are personal asset, not product asset.
findings.recommendation: Build PersonaLearner: (1) After accuracy_ratings are submitted, run weekly aggregation (persona_id, project_id, aspect, rating). (2) Detect patterns: if [CFO_v1, revenue_forecast] consistently rates 2.5/5, flag it as 'blind spot.' (3) On next project, auto-inject calibration note in persona prompt: 'This persona tends to underestimate long-tail revenue; adjust upward 20%.' (4) Store patterns in persona_calibrations table (persona_id, aspect, blind_spot_description, correction_factor). (5) UI: on PersonaForm, show 'Past accuracy: [aspect breakdown]' + 'Known blind spots: [list]' so user can decide to adjust or keep as-is.

findings.title: Argument Structure & Conviction Tracking Absent (SDD's 'Why' Gap)
findings.evidence: SDD (GitHub Spec Kit) uses '_Leverage: path_' annotations to trace every design decision back to a requirement or organizational value. Argus design_rationale (RecastItem) explains *why* a workflow structure exists, but this is free text, not executable. There's no way to query 'which decisions depend on assumption X?' or 'if we deprioritize Y, which workflow steps become optional?' Argus outputs Recast steps with task, actor, expected_output — no _Leverage annotations tracing back to Reframe phase. This makes cascade analysis impossible.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Audit checks: is design_rationale clear? Does it explain the workflow? Yes. Doesn't check: could we *mechanically query* dependencies? 'Show me all Recast steps that depend on Reframe assumption #3.' That's not a capability; it requires structured tracing (a SDD feature Argus doesn't have).
findings.impact: Decision mutations are fragile. If you update a Reframe assumption, you must manually trace which Recast steps, Personas, and Checklists are affected. SDD systems do this automatically via dependency graphs. Argus is dependency-blind.
findings.recommendation: Add Provenance Tracing: (1) Each RecastStep gets _leverage array: [{ source_type: 'reframe_assumption', ref_id: 'uuid', text: 'assumption #3' }]. (2) Add _requires_verification array (which facts must be true for this step). (3) Build DependencyGraph builder that traverses all steps, builds artifact dependency map. (4) UI: RecastStep card shows expandable 'Depends on' section. (5) Checklist export includes _leverage comments (SDD-style). (6) Query endpoint: GET /api/decision/:id/impact?assumption=uuid → returns all downstream steps/artifacts affected by that assumption.

adversary.the_one_thing: Argus's "judgment before execution" thesis is architecturally sound, but it has no way to validate that the judgment was correct — there is zero instrumentation to bind deployed decision outcomes back into the judgment loop. Phase 4 (self-improving prompts) and Phase 1 (adaptive strategies) require outcome data that never arrives. Without execution feedback, Argus becomes a *one-time structure machine* rather than a *learning system*. Users can trust it to organize thinking (domain strength), but not to improve predictions (domain weakness vs. autoresearch, which learns overnight). The fix is not cosmetic: it requires webhook instrumentation to CrewAI/LangGraph/execution systems, Supabase schema for outcome recording, and re-plumbing of eval-engine to validate against reality, not just user perception. Until then, Argus's learning loops are asymptotic — measuring user satisfaction, not decision quality.

adversary.lens: Prompt & AI-Output Quality: The Seductive Competence Trap
adversary.summary: Argus is architected around high-quality prompting (strategic, specificity-enforcing, anti-hedging). System prompts are sharp—they explicitly reject hedging ("그럴듯한 오답"), enforce authoritativeness, and link reframing to execution. Yet the stack has THREE unchecked vulnerabilities: (1) the reframing prompt's confidence scoring has no post-hoc validation against user reality; (2) multi-agent synthesis creates NEW opportunities for plausible-but-wrong consensus; (3) the evaluation suite measures STRUCTURE (has_unspoken_risk, adds_value) but not TRUTH—a brilliant-looking plan can pass all evals and still be irrelevant. The "Siren" the product warns against isn't only ChatGPT's fluent generic advice; it's also Argus's own coherent-but-disconnected analyses.

findings.title: Framing Confidence is Unvalidated Post-Hoc
findings.evidence: src/lib/progressive-prompts.ts:45–49. The initial analysis prompt asks LLM to rate 'framing_confidence' (0–100) based on 'crystal clear' vs 'too vague' criteria. This confidence score influences whether follow-up questions clarify ambiguity. But there is NO mechanism to check if the LLM's confidence prediction matches actual user reception. A 75% confidence reframe—deemed 'mostly clear, one ambiguity'—could be solving the wrong problem entirely if the ambiguity is about the user's actual underlying need, not process clarity.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A UI/correctness audit checks: 'Does confidence show on the card?' (yes). A prompt audit checks: 'Is the confidence scoring logic sound?' (yes, the rubric is reasonable). But neither tests: 'Is the LLM's confidence PREDICTIVE of user validation?' This is cross-cutting—happens at the moment of highest impact (first reframe) and compounds downstream.
findings.impact: Users can accept a 'confident' reframe that *feels* like their problem but misses the deeper question. They proceed to step 2 (recast) on a false premise. All subsequent work—execution plans, personas, rehearsal feedback—is architecturally sound but strategically irrelevant. The product's core promise ('reveal what's really at stake') fails silently because the confidence mechanism has no feedback loop.
findings.recommendation: Add a post-reframe validation checkpoint: after the user selects their reframed_question, ask a single probe—'If you had to explain this to your boss in one sentence, would that sentence be this one?' or 'What would change if this question were wrong?' Record the response as `framing_validation_signal`. If users say 'actually, I'd phrase it differently' >30% of the time for high-confidence frames, that's signal that confidence scoring is miscalibrated. Feed this back to the reframing strategy selection (lower confidence for ambiguous-origin tasks).

findings.title: Multi-Agent Synthesis Enables Plausible-But-Coherent False Consensus
findings.evidence: src/lib/lead-agent.ts:142–200. The lead agent synthesis prompt says: 'If workers contradict each other (across DIFFERENT tasks), make a judgment call and explain your reasoning.' This is designed for real synthesis. But there's no constraint preventing the lead from *creating coherence where none should exist*. Example: Worker A (research) says 'market shows 40% demand', Worker B (finance) says 'our margin model only works at 60%+ demand', Worker C (risk) says 'competitor moving down-market'. The lead synthesis could produce: 'Demand exists but at lower price point; this is a strategic repositioning opportunity.' All three workers are true; the synthesis is coherent; and the user proceeds with false confidence that the problem is solved (it's not—they don't have a 60% demand path).
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Architecture audit: 'Is lead synthesis structured well?' (yes, task grouping, frameworks, directive injection). Correctness audit: 'Does the lead synthesize all workers?' (yes). Prompt audit: 'Are synthesis directives clear?' (yes). But no audit questions: 'Does synthesis hide contradictions by reframing them as strategy?' or 'Are critical incompatibilities being masked by narrative flow?' This only surfaces when the plan hits reality and a key assumption breaks.
findings.impact: Users trust a synthesized analysis precisely because it's coherent—it reads like leadership thinking. But coherence ≠ correctness. The product positioned itself against 'the seductive song' of AI fluency; instead it can produce a *better-written seductive song*—one that's internally consistent and has multiple expert signatures, so users discount their doubts.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'contradiction highlight' step after lead synthesis: LLM scans the final synthesis and explicitly lists any findings from different workers that are *mutually exclusive or hard to reconcile* (not just different angles). Present these as flags: 'Research says demand, Finance says margin—these aren't both true unless [X]. Is [X] in your plan?' Give the user a deliberate choice to either reconcile explicitly or split the plan into two scenarios. Surface contradictions instead of burying them in narrative.

findings.title: Eval Framework Measures Structure, Not Truth (The Grifter's Loophole)
findings.evidence: src/lib/skill-quality-eval.ts:132–205. REFRAME_EVALS sample: 'frame_shift' (did the reframing change angles?), 'assumptions_non_generic' (are they project-specific?), 'blind_spot_uncomfortable' (would user say 'didn't think about that?'). All structural. None test: 'Is this reframing actually addressing a real constraint in their world?' A reframe could pass ALL evals—be specific, uncomfortable, non-generic—and still be completely disconnected from the user's actual bottleneck. Example: User is a founder worried about team retention in a startup. Reframe: 'You're not hiring a VP Eng; you're betting on whether this person stays if you get acquired for $50M.' Specific ✓, uncomfortable ✓, non-generic ✓. But if the user's *actual* issue is 'my team is overworked this sprint,' the reframe is a clever redirection, not a revelation.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Correctness audit measures: '5 evals, each has exemplar, binary yes/no, LLM judge.' That's rigorous for *what you're measuring*. But no audit questions: 'What aren't we measuring?' or 'Could a plan pass all evals and still miss the point?' The eval suite is self-contained. It never asks: 'Was the reframe VALIDATED against user reality or only against rubric categories?'
findings.impact: High-quality outputs are indistinguishable from good outputs at read time. A user sees a reframing that is clever, specific, non-generic, uncomfortable—and doesn't realize it might be addressing the wrong problem. They spend two weeks designing to this reframe, reach rehearsal, and discover the real bottleneck is something else. The product claims 'Think before you recast,' but if thinking happens in a vacuum (no reality-testing), it's GIGO with better fonts.
findings.recommendation: After each major step (reframe → recast → rehearse), add a 'reality checkpoint' prompt: Ask the user ONE non-yes/no probe: 'If you had to bet $10k on this analysis being right, what would you need to confirm first?' OR 'What part of this would your [stakeholder] disagree with?' Record their answer as a 'reality_gap_signal.' If users repeatedly say 'I'd need to talk to X' or 'I'd need to check Y,' those are blind spots the analysis missed. Aggregate these signals to retrain reframing strategy selection—certain strategies (especially 'redirect_angle') may produce high-quality-feeling outputs that don't align with user reality.

findings.title: Persona Feedback Lacks Conflict-Density Check (Rehearsal Becomes Affirmation)
findings.evidence: src/lib/persona-prompt.ts:101–134. Persona feedback intensity is 'soft / honest / harsh.' The prompt says: 'This is a 3-min corridor conversation' (soft) or '10-min meeting feedback' (harsh). But intensity is USER-SELECTED. And the evals (src/lib/skill-quality-eval.ts:231–236) only check 'makes_uncomfortable'—one data point. There's no check for: 'Is ANY persona actually going to kill the plan?' If the user sets all personas to 'honest' or 'soft' and the feedback comes back as 'direction is good, a few tweaks here,' the user has NOT heard what they need to hear. They've heard affirmation wrapped in constructive language.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: UX audit: 'Can user adjust intensity?' (yes). Prompt audit: 'Are personas voice-acted authentically?' (yes). But no audit questions: 'Is the rehearsal actually catching veto points?' or 'Would a real CFO/CEO in this scenario actually say NO?' A robust rehearsal should produce at least ONE finding that makes the user reconsider direction; otherwise it's theater.
findings.impact: The product's core value is to catch 'the plan would fail if X goes wrong.' Rehearsal should surface that X. But if personas are weak or user-selected to be kind, rehearsal becomes a morale boost instead of a pressure test. Users graduate to 'refine' thinking they've pressure-tested, when they've only fact-checked.
findings.recommendation: Add an automatic 'Intensity Calibration' flag: After personas generate feedback, LLM scans it for severity distribution. If all feedback is 'minor' or 'soft,' flag: 'No critical risks surfaced. This could mean [a] the plan is sound, or [b] personas were too lenient.' Offer user a 're-rehearsal with higher intensity' button. OR: Automatically inject one 'veto-scale persona' (different from user selections) whose only job is to find the one critical failure mode. Make it clear this persona isn't replacing user-selected ones; it's a supplemental 'devil's advocate' that runs in the background. Ensure at least one high-severity finding appears in every rehearsal.

findings.title: No Feedback Loop from Execution Reality Back to Prompting (Analysis Pyramid Frozen)
findings.evidence: The architecture (ROADMAP.md Phase 4) includes 'Eval Framework' for recording binary pass/fail metrics. But: (1) binary evals are recorded only IF user completes a project (status='done'). (2) There is NO mechanism to feed back 'did your reframed question actually matter?' or 'did any of the key assumptions break?' (3) Even if these signals existed, they don't influence the system prompts—only the strategy selection (src/lib/eval-engine.ts:189–195). The system prompts themselves are static.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Architecture audit sees the eval framework and strategy selection as complete. Correctness audit checks that evals are recorded. But neither asks: 'Are we learning from failures?' or 'Do users who selected 'challenge_existence' and then had to backtrack teach the system anything?' The feedback loop is architecturally disconnected from the prompt layer.
findings.impact: The product can't correct its own output quality over time. If a reframing strategy consistently produces high-confidence frames that users later say 'actually that wasn't the issue,' the system never learns to de-weight that strategy for that context. The prompts stay the same, so the same mistakes repeat. The learning is one-way: user practice → better judgment. The AI doesn't get better at helping.
findings.recommendation: Implement a Supabase table `outcome_validations`: After a project completes, send the user a single async question: 'Of the assumptions we identified, which one actually mattered? Which one turned out not to matter?' Record their response linked to the original reframe/strategy. Then add a 'strategy_effectiveness' score: for each (strategy, context) pair, compute % of projects where the user said 'yes, that was the real question' vs 'no, we pivoted.' This becomes feedback into `selectReframingStrategy()` with 50+ samples per pattern. Update system prompts annually based on which strategies produce outcomes users validate. Make this visible to the user: 'This reframing strategy worked well in [N] similar situations.' Closes the feedback loop.

findings.title: Progressive Engine Generates Outputs Faster Than User Certainty Can Keep Up
findings.evidence: src/lib/progressive-engine.ts calls `runTypedQuestion()` with round limits (default maxRounds: 6–8). Each round takes ~30–60 seconds of LLM time. By round 3, the system has a full execution plan with step actors, checkpoints, and key assumptions. By round 5, it's generating worker task assignments. The UX is: new insight on each round (compels users to keep going). But research on decision velocity suggests that once a plan is 'coherent enough,' users stop scrutinizing it. They proceed to execution. The product accelerates toward a plan, but doesn't force the user to slow down when certainty is low.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: UX audit: 'Do users understand each step?' (yes). Prompt audit: 'Are questions good?' (yes). But no audit of: 'Is the system going too FAST relative to user confidence growth?' This is a pacing problem, not a quality problem—orthogonal to normal domain audits.
findings.impact: Users move from 'I have a vague question' (round 0) to 'I have a detailed plan' (round 5) in 5 minutes. The human learning curve isn't that fast. They feel swept along. Then they hit refine/rehearsal and realize there are gaps they didn't catch. But by then they're attached to the plan. The product's speed becomes a liability: it makes users *feel* confident before they *are* confident.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Certainty Checkpoint' at round 3: Ask the user: 'On a scale, how confident are you in the direction (not the details)?' If <60%, pause progress. Don't move to execution plan until user says 'yes, I'm confident in the direction.' If the user is uncertain, offer a branching: 'Try a different reframing?' or 'Go deeper on current frame?' (add 2 more Q&A rounds). Decouple plan completeness from question rounds—allow the user to say 'I think I have it' at round 2 or 'I need more' at round 4. Make the tool responsive to user certainty, not just process completion.

adversary.the_one_thing: **The Confidence Trap**: The product's reframing step asks the LLM to self-assess confidence (0–100) on whether the reframed question is the RIGHT question. This confidence influences downstream strategy. But there is ZERO post-hoc validation. A high-confidence reframe proceeds directly to execution design—with no requirement that the user validate whether the frame actually matches their world. The product can generate a brilliant, specific, uncomfortable reframe that passes all structural evals and still be solving the wrong problem. Users don't realize it until they've spent a week on the plan. The "Siren's song" the product warns against isn't defeated; it's just better-written.

surface.lens: Claude Code Skills & Plugin Surface — Cross-version drift, branding incoherence, and maintenance burden across two parallel plugin architectures
surface.summary: Argus ships **two fundamentally incompatible Claude Code plugins** (`argus-plugin` v0.5 and `argus-plugin-v2` v2.0.0) that compete for the same user surface. The old plugin (v0.5) uses the voyage/4R metaphor (reframe → recast → rehearse → refine) and produces markdown contracts; the new plugin (v2.0.0) uses orchestration vocabulary (sail → clarify → team → boss) with JSON schemas. The README correctly points users to v2, but v1 still exists in the repo with live install.sh and no deprecation warnings. Skills in `.claude/` mix both vocabularies: `/orchestrate` (dead, aliased to `/recast`), `/recast` (voyage), and legacy 4R skills coexist. The web app uses voyage branding exclusively (per philosophy doc) but the plugin ecosystem hasn't synchronized — v1 and v2 represent two different product eras, both partially complete.

findings.title: Two competing plugins with incompatible branding and install paths
findings.evidence: argus-plugin/install.sh (line 169-191, verifies argus/reframe/recast/rehearse/refine) vs argus-plugin-v2/install.sh (line 172, verifies sail/clarify/team/boss/chart). README.md line 146 recommends v2 install. Both plugin.json files exist with v0.5 vs v2.0.0 declarations.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A domain-focused audit (code quality, reliability, UI/UX) would evaluate each plugin in isolation. Cross-cutting issues only appear when asking 'which plugin should a user actually install?' — that's an end-to-end product decision, not a per-domain concern.
findings.impact: Users who follow old tutorials or find argus-plugin/ first will install v0.5, which uses 4R voyage language. Users of the web app already know /argus/reframe/recast/rehearse/refine. But Claude Code users are now pointed to /argus:sail/clarify/team/boss (completely different). Confusion between 'should I use v1 or v2?' is unresolved. Support burden: must maintain TWO skill trees.
findings.recommendation: Immediately delete argus-plugin/ directory OR (safer) rename to argus-plugin-legacy/ and add a DEPRECATION.md at the root explaining the swap. Update all references in docs to clarify v2 is canonical. If v1 is to stay, add a MIGRATION.md that maps old skill names to new ones (e.g., 'if you learned /recast, use /argus:clarify → /argus:team instead').

findings.title: Dead/orphaned skills in .claude/skills — /orchestrate is a zombie alias
findings.evidence: .claude/skills/orchestrate/SKILL.md (lines 1-22): descriptor says 'Alias for /recast. Use /recast instead' and explicitly routes users away. This skill exists but is anti-useful — its only purpose is to tell users not to use it. SKILL.md exists but should not be installed.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Skill installation happens at the repo level (skills-lock.json, install.sh). A domain-focused code review of workflow components would never see the orchestrate skill because it's a pure redirect. Dead code detection requires searching the full skills directory and understanding user intent.
findings.impact: If a user has both .claude/skills/orchestrate and .claude/skills/recast installed, `/orchestrate` and `/recast` do different things (orchestrate sends you to recast; recast runs directly). Message 'Use /recast instead' creates friction on every misclick. More broadly, this signals that v1→v2 migration is incomplete.
findings.recommendation: Delete .claude/skills/orchestrate/ entirely. If backward compatibility is critical, keep the SKILL.md but make it DRY: it currently duplicates routing logic that recast should own. Better: add a DEPRECATED_SKILLS.md at repo root listing what moved/changed in the v1→v2 swap.

findings.title: Plugin-v2 is undocumented for version parity with web app; voyage metaphor nowhere in CLI plugin
findings.evidence: argus-plugin-v2/README.md (line 5, 159-170) uses 'decision scaffold' + agent team language; never mentions 'voyage' or '항로/선원/리허설/항로수정'. Web app philosophy doc (Argus_Product_Philosophy_v2.md, line 1) is built entirely on voyage metaphor with 항로 재설정 → 선원 배치 → 리허설 → 항로 수정 → 이타카. Plugin-v2 README does NOT mention this framing. Users learning from web app docs will use voyage language; plugin-v2 skill docs use agent/worker language. Metaphor is lost in translation.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Metaphorical consistency is a cross-product concern. A UX audit of the plugin alone would find it coherent (sail/clarify/team/boss is internally consistent). A product philosophy audit of the web app alone would find voyage is well-integrated. The blind spot is the HANDOFF: what do users see when they switch surfaces?
findings.impact: Users see two different conceptual models of the same product. Web app describes 'selecting a hidden assumption in step 1 triggers it to appear in step 2's key_assumptions' — journey metaphor, causality visible. Plugin describes 'clarify() produces analysis-snapshot → team() consumes and deploys agents'. Same logic, totally different narrative. Users migrate between surfaces confused.
findings.recommendation: Add a 'Mapping: Voyage to Plugin' section in argus-plugin-v2/README.md (before §5) that explains: '항로 재설정 = clarify (sharpening the question), 선원 배치 = team (workers on artifacts), 리허설 = boss review, 항로 수정 = chart + revise'. Make the conceptual bridge explicit for users coming from web app.

findings.title: Dual data models (markdown contracts vs JSON schemas) — no sync, two sources of truth
findings.evidence: argus-plugin/CONTEXT-CONTRACT.md (lines 25-150): defines reframe/recast/rehearse/refine markdown output format (.argus/reframe.md, .argus/recast.md, etc.). argus-plugin-v2/data/schemas/*.json: defines analysis-snapshot.json, final-scaffold.json, worker-result.json, etc. Both plugin.json files list DIFFERENT references: v1 points to CONTEXT-CONTRACT.md; v2 points to data/schemas/*.json and lib/. NO conversion layer between them. If v1 generates .argus/recast.md and v2 expects .argus/sessions/{id}/versions/{label}/workers.json, they cannot read each other's output.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: A web-app audit would examine Zustand stores (types.ts shows typed ContextChain). A plugin audit would examine SKILL.md files. Neither would catch that the *integration point* (.argus/ directory) has two incompatible data structures. The blind spot is at the filesystem level, not code quality.
findings.impact: If a user installs v2 plugin, runs /argus:sail, then tries to use v1 skills (because they learned the old names), the skills cannot read v2's JSON output. Worse: upgrade path is broken. Teams using v1 cannot migrate to v2 without losing session history (data is in .argus/*.md format, v2 expects .argus/sessions/*/versions/*/). No migration script. Data loss risk.
findings.recommendation: Write a migration utility: .argus/migrate-v1-to-v2.ts (or similar) that reads v1 markdown contracts and converts to v2 JSON schema. Ship it as part of argus-plugin-v2/install.sh with a pre-flight check: 'Found v1 session data. Migrate? (Y/n)' — this is critical for any team that's been using v1.

findings.title: Missing forward-compatibility signals in .claude/skills — no version pinning, no deprecation notices
findings.evidence: .claude/skills/ contains both v0.5-era skills (reframe, recast, rehearse, refine) and utility skills (setup, doctor, patterns). None of these SKILL.md files have a version field or deprecation notice indicating they are for v0.5 and should not be used alongside v2. argus-plugin-v2/install.sh will overwrite ~/.claude/skills/{name} with v2 versions, but there's NO WARNING about version incompatibility or explicit 'uninstall v1 first' instruction.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Installation and version management happen at the repo/CI boundary, not in component code. A code review would see the skill .md files are well-written. But 'how do we signal which versions are compatible?' is a product operations concern, not domain-specific.
findings.impact: If a user has .claude/skills/recast from v0.5 and installs v2 plugin on top, the new /argus:sail will reference .claude/skills/recast, but that recast skill expects .argus/recast.md format (v1 contract). Skill fails or produces garbage. No error handling, no clear failure message.
findings.recommendation: Add a version field to all SKILL.md headers. Example: `version: 0.5.0` or `version: 2.0.0`. Update install.sh to check for version conflicts: 'Detected v0.5 recast skill + v2.0 install conflict. Abort? (Y/n)'. Add a .claude/VERSION.txt file that tracks installed plugin version globally.

findings.title: Plugin-v2 BUILD_STATUS.md is comprehensive but not user-facing; v1 has no build status
findings.evidence: argus-plugin-v2/BUILD_STATUS.md is 255 lines, documents 20 bug fixes, 10 meta-checks, test cases, and build confidence (92%). It's a developer document. But users installing v2 see no indication of maturity. argus-plugin/ has NO BUILD_STATUS or RELEASE_NOTES. v1 is version 0.5.0 (release candidate signal), v2 is 2.0.0 (major version, implies stable), yet v2 only reached 92% build confidence while v1 has been in the wild longer.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Release readiness and confidence signals are product/ops concerns, not code quality. A code review of v2 skills would find them well-specified. A UX review of v2 README would find it clear. But 'what signals maturity/stability to users?' is an audience-specific cross-cutting concern.
findings.impact: Users assume v2.0.0 is 'stable, use it confidently'. But seeing BUILD_STATUS mentions '8% uncertainty at integration boundaries, schema $ref cross-resolution untested, install.sh path resolution untested' should make them cautious. v1 users don't know what to expect from the migration. No confidence scoring is public.
findings.recommendation: Add a STABILITY.md at the repo root (or enhance README §2) listing: v0.5 (in field, stable, maintenance-only), v2.0.0 (build confidence 92%, known limitations: ...). Add release notes for v2 with known issues and testing status. Link to TEST_PLAN.md from v2 README so users can see what was validated.

findings.title: Agents are shared between v1 and v2 but not versioned; voice preservation claims may not hold
findings.evidence: Both plugin.json files list agents/ directory with 17-18 agent .md files (hayoon.md, sujin.md, donghyuk.md, etc.). argus-plugin/agents/ and argus-plugin-v2/agents/ both claim the same agent names. BUILD_STATUS.md (line 44-45) claims M2 (Personality preservation): 'all current files show rhythm/tone examples'. But these files have been edited multiple times across v1→v2 transition. No agent version tracking. If v1 agents have been silently updated to match v2 expectations, v1 skills may be broken. If they differ, which is canonical?
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Voice/personality audit would examine agent .md files in isolation. Without checking git history or diffs, you can't see if agents were updated mid-refactor. The product philosophy assumes agents are stable, but the technical reality (two plugins trying to use the same agents) is fragile.
findings.impact: Agent voice consistency is critical for Argus credibility. If hayoon.md was tweaked to match v2's 'worker mode' style but still lives in both plugins, v1 users get the v2-tuned version. The claimed voice preservation in BUILD_STATUS may not apply retrospectively. Risk: agent personality shifts without user noticing, breaking implicit contracts in stored sessions.
findings.recommendation: Add agent version metadata to each agent .md file (e.g., `agent_version: 1.0.0` at the top). In install.sh, validate that installed agents match the plugin version. Or: move agents into version-specific directories (agents-v1/, agents-v2/) and symlink appropriately during install.

findings.title: README.md recommends v2 but docstrings in .claude/skills still use old metaphor
findings.evidence: .claude/skills/reframe/SKILL.md (line 3): 'Sharpen your question before asking AI.' — generic, no voyage reference. .claude/skills/recast/SKILL.md (line 3): 'Design AI/human roles after planning' — also generic. But Argus_Product_Philosophy_v2.md (line 62) requires 'Reframe' to be framed as '항로 재설정' / 'Set the Heading'. The philosophy doc says: '항해 어휘는 업무명과 항상 병기한다' (voyage metaphor must always pair with business task). Installed skills violate this principle.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Branding consistency (metaphor application) is not a code-quality or feature-completeness issue. It's a narrative/product-voice concern. A component audit would see reframe.md is well-written; a branding audit would see the philosophy doc is internally consistent. The gap is in APPLYING the philosophy to shipping artifacts.
findings.impact: New users who read the philosophy doc, then use /reframe, see no connection. They don't learn the voyage metaphor; it stays invisible in code. This weakens the product narrative and makes the learning curve steeper (why am I doing this in 4 steps? The metaphor explains 'it's like a voyage'). Experienced users expect consistent framing across all surfaces.
findings.recommendation: Update all .claude/skills/*/SKILL.md description fields to include voyage context. Example: 'reframe' should say 'Set the Heading — sharpen your question before asking AI.' Update SKILL.md headers to reference the phase of the voyage. This is a text-only fix, high-signal for coherence.

findings.title: install.sh scripts are nearly identical but hardcoded for different skill sets — DRY violation, maintenance risk
findings.evidence: argus-plugin/install.sh and argus-plugin-v2/install.sh share ~90% of code (color functions, platform detection, symlink logic). But line 169 (v1) and line 172 (v2) have incompatible skill name lists. Any fix to symlink creation, error handling, or install paths must be duplicated in both. No shared library.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Code duplication is usually caught by domain-focused linters/reviews. But when duplication spans two separate directories with different purposes (v1 vs v2), it doesn't trigger alerts. The blind spot is 'same code, different intent'.
findings.impact: If a bug is found in symlink creation (e.g., Windows path escaping), it must be fixed in both install.sh files. Risk of divergence: v2 gets the fix, v1 doesn't, and v1 users hit the bug. Maintenance burden scales quadratically with changes.
findings.recommendation: Extract shared install logic to scripts/install-common.sh (functions: check_claude_dir, symlink_skill, verify_skills). Both install.sh files source it. Keep version-specific lists (skill names, required plugins) in the caller. This is a standard refactor.

surface.the_one_thing: **Two incompatible plugin versions coexist with zero transition path.** Users are pointed to v2 in the README, but v0.5 is still in the repo with a live install.sh and no deprecation warning. The two plugins use different skill names (v1: /reframe→/recast→/rehearse→/refine vs v2: /clarify→/team→/boss), produce different data structures (.md contracts vs JSON schemas), and don't inter-operate. There's no migration utility, no version conflict detection, and no clear 'if you're on v1, here's how to move to v2'. A user who installs v2 after using v1 will lose session history and face confusing skill errors. This is a **product versioning crisis disguised as technical debt** — the web app shipped voyage branding, plugin-v1 implements it, but plugin-v2 invented new metaphors (orchestrator, team, workers) and the README quietly points users there without explaining the break. The blind spot: domain audits of v1 and v2 in isolation miss that there's no world in which both should exist simultaneously shipping to the same user base.

surface.lens: Data Lifecycle & Longevity: Storage schema evolution, multi-device sync, unbounded growth, data deletion/export, and the invisible accumulation patterns across years
surface.summary: Argus has a robust local-first sync architecture and thoughtful data capping for discrete types. But cross-cutting data lifecycle is fragile: progressive sessions grow unbounded; timestamp-based merge is vulnerable to clock skew; no versioning for schema changes; soft-deletes accumulate forever; quality signals pile up without learning loops. Works flawlessly for first 10 sessions, but integrity/performance/privacy risks emerge at scale (100+ sessions, multi-device, concurrent edits). Domain audits see 'error handling exists' and 'caps are in place' without testing: week 50 of heavy use, localStorage exceeds quota, edits fail silently, users lose work.

findings.title: localStorage Quota Exhaustion
findings.evidence: useProgressiveStore.ts:1369; storage.ts:37-44
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Components tested in isolation. Signal cap (500), eval cap (200) exist. But central session object (questions, answers, snapshots, workers×8 branches, checkpoints) grows unbounded. User with 10 sessions × 8 branches × 50 checkpoints each hits quota. No test checks localStorage exceeds 5MB.
findings.impact: Week 50: edits silently fail. UI appears to save. On reload, work is lost. Sync breaks.
findings.recommendation: Per-user cap (max 20 sessions) + per-session budget (2MB). Checkpoint pruning. Quota meter. Change setStorage to throw/toast. Supabase alerts.

findings.title: mergeByTimestamp Clock Skew Vulnerability
findings.evidence: db.ts:57-78 uses `if (remoteTime > localTime)` on ISO strings
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Correctness audit: 'does merge keep items?' yes. Doesn't test: Device A edits at 14:30:00Z, Device B clock 2m fast, user's edit at 14:31:00Z loses to Device B's 'newer' remote. No E2E with clock drift.
findings.impact: Silent data loss: user's recent work overwritten by stale Device B data with faster clock. No recovery if happens to final_deliverable.
findings.recommendation: Three-way merge with edit logs. Fallback to 'both' when within 1s. Monotonic sequences. CRDT for critical fields.

findings.title: No Versioning for Schema Changes
findings.evidence: types.ts has backward-compat comments but no STORAGE_VERSION; migrations ad-hoc
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Domains handle missing fields gracefully via defaults. But if v2 adds field, 1000+ v1 items lack it. Fallback works, no re-analysis path.
findings.impact: New features depend on new data; old projects silently lack it. Features break. Users must recreate projects.
findings.recommendation: Add STORAGE_VERSION stamp. Run versioned migrations on load. Add schema_version to Supabase. 'Re-analyze' button.

findings.title: No Granular Data Deletion or Export
findings.evidence: db.ts softDeleteFromSupabase marks deleted_at but never purges; deleteAllUserData is all-or-nothing
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Privacy audit: 'can delete?' yes. Misses: user wants to delete sessions 1-50, keep 51-100. No selective UI. Deleted sessions accumulate forever.
findings.impact: No granular privacy control. GDPR non-compliant. Deleted rows grow unbounded.
findings.recommendation: Per-project delete with export offer. Hard-delete after 90 days. Cron cleanup. 'Download my data'.

findings.title: Concurrent Session Edits Merge Naively
findings.evidence: useProgressiveStore branches as array; mergeByTimestamp at item level; JSONB monolithic
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Audit: 'branches preserved?' yes. Doesn't test: Device A adds branch X, Device B adds branch Y, both edit checkpoint. One overwrites.
findings.impact: Collaborative edits lose work. One analyst's checkpoint silently overwritten.
findings.recommendation: Per-branch timestamps. Last-write-wins for non-overlapping. Conflict UI. Version vectors.

findings.title: Quality Signals No Feedback Loop
findings.evidence: signal-recorder.ts records capped 500; eval-engine never reads; Phase 4 not implemented
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Infra: 'recorded?' yes. E2E: 'Do signals inform strategy?' Not yet. Loop incomplete, invisible.
findings.impact: Thousands of rows accumulate. Never analyzed. Storage cost, zero return.
findings.recommendation: Complete Phase 4: signal dashboard, strategy weight adjustment. 6-month expiry.

findings.title: Unvalidated JSONB in Supabase
findings.evidence: migrations/20260409 creates RLS with untyped JSONB data; no schema check
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Security: RLS works. Data structure: type defined. Neither asks: does Supabase validate JSONB conforms to TS?
findings.impact: Malformed JSON corrupts session. Client crashes, no trail.
findings.recommendation: Check constraint validating JSON. Validate responses. Test malformed JSON.

findings.title: No Retention for Evaluation Logs
findings.evidence: eval-engine caps localStorage at 200; inserts to Supabase with no TTL or cron
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Efficiency: storage efficient. Doesn't ask: does data expire? No policy. Invisible until millions of rows.
findings.impact: After 2 years, queries slow. Costs increase.
findings.recommendation: Cron: delete > 1 year. Keep quality_scores. Trim button. Row alerts.

surface.the_one_thing: localStorage quota exhaustion with no safeguard. Week 50: edit fails silently (console-only), user reloads, work lost. Combines (1) unbounded session growth, (2) silent catch swallowing QuotaExceededError, (3) zero UI feedback. For a tool built on 'judgment before execution', losing work without warning betrays core philosophy.

surface.summary: Argus has a sophisticated analytics and eval-engine infrastructure (analytics.ts, signal-recorder.ts, eval-engine.ts) that correctly captures ~50 distinct user events and binary eval signals. However, CRITICAL disconnect: 7 of 9 ROADMAP success metrics are unmeasurable in production. The product is flying blind on whether it's achieving its core strategic goals. Example: ROADMAP defines 'reframing adoption >60%' and 'persona accuracy avg >3.5/5', but no SQL query exists to measure either. Eval results are collected locally, never surfaced as product dashboards. Output usage is untracked (users copy/download outputs? unknown). Loop convergence iterations are invisible. This creates a measurement gap: analytics layer is well-engineered but disconnected from strategy. Team can see raw events in Supabase but has no lenses to answer 'are we winning?'

findings.title: ROADMAP Success Metrics Unmeasurable: 7 of 9 Metrics Have No Query
findings.evidence: ROADMAP.md §5 defines 9 success metrics (reframing adoption >60%, proceed-to-recast >70%, assumption verification >0.5/session, persona accuracy >3.5/5, output usage >40%, revisit >50%, convergence <3 iterations, coda reflection >20%, completion >30%). Only 2 are measurable: completion (flow_done event query exists in daily report), and persona accuracy (ratings collected but never aggregated). Missing: adoption %, assumption engagement, output usage, revisit rate, convergence iterations, reflection rate. src/lib/analytics.ts and src/lib/eval-engine.ts have NO SQL pattern to compute these.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Domain audits (reliability, UX, visual design) test whether individual features work (do assumption checkboxes function? yes). But 'is this metric achievable and measurable?' is orthogonal to feature correctness. A developer audit sees eval-engine.ts working perfectly; evals are recorded, stored, and locally readable. But nobody asked: are these evals surfaced to the team? Are they aggregated? Are they connected to product strategy? The gap is between 'data exists' and 'data is visible to decision-makers'.
findings.impact: Team cannot validate whether Phase 1-2 improvements are working. Did reframing adoption go from 40% → 65% after last prompt change? Unknown. Is persona accuracy improving as users provide feedback? Unknown. Has refinement loop convergence slowed (bad signal)? Unknown. Decisions become folklore-based ('users seemed to love X') instead of data-driven. Cannot justify continued investment in areas without metrics.
findings.recommendation: Create 1-page Supabase SQL dashboard for each ROADMAP metric (7 queries, 4 hours). Example: 'SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT item_id) as total, COUNT(DISTINCT item_id) FILTER (WHERE user_edited_question=false) as adopted FROM reframe_items WHERE status='done' GROUP BY DATE(created_at)' gives daily adoption rate. Wire each to daily_report or Supabase alerts if metric crosses red line.

findings.title: Assumption Engagement Untracked: Phase 1 Core Engagement Signal Lost
findings.evidence: eval-engine.ts REFRAME_EVALS line 58-65: 'assumptions_engaged' eval measures if user marked ≥1 assumption as likely_true/doubtful/uncertain. This is collected into localStorage eval history. ROADMAP metric: 'avg assumptions verified >0.5/session.' But NO track() call emitted when assumption is verified/marked. No aggregation query exists. Daily report has zero reference to assumption engagement metrics. User marking an assumption is a core product signal that should be public, not buried in internal eval tuples.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: UI audit: assumption checkboxes work. Backend audit: assumptions are persisted correctly. But the signal 'user engaged with this assumption and evaluated it' is treated as an internal learning signal (used for strategy selection), not a product health metric (visible to team). The blindspot is the seam between 'signal collected' and 'signal surfaced.' Code is correct; visibility is missing.
findings.impact: Cannot validate Argus's core promise: 'users discover hidden assumptions.' If assumption engagement is actually 0.1/session instead of 0.5, Argus is failing silently. The assumption-evaluation UI could be ignored by users for months before anyone notices because no metric tracks it.
findings.recommendation: Add track('assumption_marked', { assumption_id, evaluation, axis, project_id }) when user rates assumption. Create daily aggregation: COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE event_name='assumption_marked') / COUNT(DISTINCT project_id) gives avg per-session rate. Surface as 'Assumption Engagement' in daily report. Goal >0.5/session.

findings.title: Output Usage Completely Untracked: Copy/Download/Revisit Events Missing
findings.evidence: OutputSelector.tsx fires track('output_generated', { format }). But NO events for: user copies output, user downloads output, user revisits an old output. ROADMAP metrics: 'output usage >40%', 'revisit >50%', 'coda write >20%'. Daily report queries 'flow_done' but that's 'output was created,' not 'output was consumed.' Zero visibility into whether outputs are actually used or sit ignored in browser tabs.
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Component audit: OutputSelector UI is well-designed, output markdown rendering is beautiful, copy button works. Functional audit: system correctly generates outputs. But the consumer-side signal—did external world (Coda, email, etc.) actually *use* this artifact—is completely unmeasured. This is the seam between Argus's internal state and external consumption. System is correct; market signal is invisible.
findings.impact: Cannot distinguish: (a) outputs are generated but ignored, (b) outputs are generated and heavily used. These require different fixes: (a) means artifact quality is wrong, (b) means generation is working. Currently shipping blind. Likely cause of user churn: spent 30min in Argus, generated output, tried to paste into Coda, format was wrong, never returned. But this pattern would never be detected.
findings.recommendation: Add event listeners: track('output_copied', { format, output_id, char_count }) on copy; track('output_downloaded', { format, output_id }) on download; track('output_revisited', { output_id, days_since_creation }) when user re-opens an old output. Daily report: 'copy rate %', 'download rate %', 'revisit rate %' per output format.

findings.title: Refinement Loop Convergence Speed Invisible: Iteration Count Never Surfaced
findings.evidence: track('loop_converged') fires but emits NO data on how many iterations happened. ROADMAP goal: 'refinement loop convergence <3 iterations.' Code has assessConvergence() in progressive-convergence.ts but iteration count is stored in progressive_sessions.data (opaque JSON blob), never extracted. Daily report has no convergence speed metric. No way to detect if loops are taking 6 iterations (bad) vs. 1.5 iterations (good).
findings.why_a_domain_audit_misses_this: Functional audit: refinement loop works—user submits feedback, system re-runs, output improves. User can *see* convergence % increase in UI.
